Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**Wireframe-fidelity exception, stated rather than silent (per CLAUDE.md's rule).** `9-MainAppHomeScreen.svg` specifies the status groups as plain, non-interactive bands with no collapse affordance. The founder ask (Bhavya, 2026-08-05) is the authority, per the standing rule that founder decisions outrank a literal wireframe reading; the full decision record is in `docs/sonny-founder-design-decisions.md` under "Tasks page — collapsible status sections". The exception is bounded to the smallest possible shape: the chevron is the only addition, it is **trailing** so the wireframe's title/count position and every band measurement stay untouched, and its treatment is copied from the two System A chevrons that already exist (`SonnyType.icon(9, weight: .semibold)`, `SonnyTheme.muted`, trailing-aligned). One practical note for whoever verifies this: **the wireframe SVG exports are not tracked in this repository** — `find . -iname '*.svg'` returns nothing — so this claim rests on the ticket and on the existing in-code wireframe comments, not on a re-read of the file.

**The running indicator is exempt from collapse — user decision, 2026-08-06, PR #31 review F1.** The first implementation gated `CommandCenterRunningIndicator` on the "In Progress" section's `isExpanded`. That was in-contract (the description says *every* status section header gains a chevron) and still wrong, for a reason worth carrying forward: **that indicator holds the app's only stop control for a plain running task.** Enumerated rather than assumed — `cancelCurrentRun()` has exactly three call sites in the whole repository, `CommandCenterView.swift:558` (the indicator's own Cancel), `CommandCenterView.swift:792` (`CommandCenterAttentionPanel`'s Deny) and `FloatingWidgetView.swift:369` (the widget's `onDeny`), and the latter two fire only on an approval. So a run that is merely executing has one cancel affordance, on this page, inside that view. Gating it on a *persisted* preference meant one click could remove it from every future run on the Tasks page, silently and permanently. The decision: the indicator renders on `isRunning || isAwaitingApproval` regardless of collapse; collapsing folds away the section's task rows only. The generalization: **the indicator convention exists so that a running task always shows something — a persisted display preference must never be able to switch that off.** A consequence recorded rather than glossed: the "In Progress" section has no task rows today, so collapsing it now changes nothing on screen beyond the chevron's rotation and the stored preference. The chevron stays because the description contracts one on every status header, and because the state is already the right shape for the day that section gains rows.

**Prose about hidden UI carries the same enumerate-then-subtract duty as a measurement.** Both places that described F1's consequence failed it in the same way: the code comment said collapsing "hides the running indicator, not the fact that something is running", and this entry said it "hides the running indicator and nothing else". Both were true about *view identity* and both misled about *what the user loses*, because neither named the Cancel button and the running command's text living inside the view being hidden. `CLAUDE.md`'s rule is written about claims generally, not about numbers specifically — a sentence that says what is *not* hidden is a subtraction, and it needs the enumeration first.

**Persist the collapsed set, never the expanded set.** The default is "everything expanded," and only a collapsed-set representation makes an absent or empty preference mean exactly that. It matters more here than it looks: `TaskHistoryGrouping.groupedByOutcome` drops empty sections, so a section genuinely does not exist until it has a record, and an expanded-set representation would have to enumerate every section that could ever exist or silently collapse each new one the first time it appeared. The same reasoning is why an unknown identifier in the persisted array is carried harmlessly rather than treated as corruption.

**The collapse preference deliberately does not live on `AgentViewModel`.** The two existing plain-`UserDefaults` preferences (`usePointerCursors`, `displayFullNames`) are there because both the widget and Command Center read them. Nothing outside this one page reads this one, so putting it on the shared view model would add `@Published` state with exactly one observer. `TaskSectionCollapseStore` is injected into `TasksFoundationView` instead, defaulted to `.standard`, which is also what makes the round-trip testable without constructing a whole view model. The rule that actually mattered — plain `UserDefaults`, not `LocalStorageEncryption`, for a cosmetic preference — is followed.

**Seed `@State` in `init`, not in `onAppear`.** `TasksFoundationView.onAppear` already fires on every return to the page (it calls `refreshTaskHistory`), so loading the preference there would re-read defaults on every tab switch and, if a write ever lagged, discard an in-session collapse. `State(initialValue: collapseStore.load())` in a custom `init` seeds once per view identity and leaves the existing `TasksFoundationView(viewModel:)` call site unchanged.

**`count` is a property of the section, not of what got rendered.** The count-while-collapsed requirement is one line away from being wrong — `section.visibleRecords.count` compiles and reads naturally and silently shows 0 on every collapsed section. Putting `count` on `TaskSectionPresentation` as `section.records.count`, independent of `isExpanded`, is what makes that mistake a test failure instead of a manual-QA discovery. Mutating it to follow the collapse state reddens 3 tests.

**Mutation battery, re-run in full and measured at `7e927e6`** — one SHA, one test population, after both rebases. Twelve mutations of `TaskSectionCollapsePresentation.swift`, each run against the full flagged 513-test suite, each red (exit 1). Distinct test functions reddened, in brackets: invert `isExpanded` [13], `toggle` to a no-op [9], invert `setExpanded` [10], `load` ignoring the stored value [3], `save` writing nothing [3], `save` dropping `.sorted()` [1], a different `defaultsKey` string [1], `count` following the collapse state [3], collapse no longer hiding rows [3], `sections(for:collapse:)` ignoring the collapse state [3], `inProgressSectionID` drifting from the header title it renders [3], `visibleRecords` reversing the grouping's order [1].

**Why the battery was re-run rather than carried forward, and why the first count reads 13 and not the 12 this entry used to state.** Two separate SHA-anchoring effects, both worth knowing. The [12] was measured when the test file held 18 `@Test` functions; `anExpandedSectionHandsBackTheGroupingsRecordsInOrder` was added afterwards and also reddens under an inverted `isExpanded`, so the same mutation over the finished 19-test file is [13]. Nothing regressed — a new pin reddening an old mutation is the pin working, exactly the effect the SONNY-24 entry documents. Separately, the rebase onto `cf99826` brought real code (23 tests, 2 suites) into the suite the battery runs against, so the old counts described a population that no longer exists. They *should* have been unaffected — `feature/automation-store-hardening` touched `RoutineSchedule`/`AutomationStores` and nothing that references `TaskSectionCollapse*` — but "should have been" is an assertion, and the whole point of the rule is that a count measured against a moved tree cannot be told apart from a stale one. Re-running twelve mutations is cheap; asserting invariance is not evidence.

Known limitations / deferred scope:
- **The view wiring is not test-pinned, only the presentation type is — four lines, across two different acceptance criteria, and every one of them fails silently.** The presentation type is pinned hard (twelve mutations, all red). Nothing pins the view that calls it, because this repository has no view-rendering tests and no view-inspection dependency. The complete enumeration, each confirmed green-under-mutation by PR #31's cycle-1 reviewer at `fc8b66f`, with line numbers at this branch's head:
  1. `State(initialValue: collapseStore.load())` (`CommandCenterView.swift:404`) — seed a fresh `TaskSectionCollapseState()` instead and the preference is never *read back*.
  2. `collapseStore.save(collapseState)` (`:506`) — drop it and the preference is never *written*. (1) and (2) each break **"collapse state persists across launches"** on their own, which is a *different* criterion from the count passthrough this paragraph originally discussed — the reason the enumeration had to be extended rather than reworded.
  3. `count: section.count` (`:1412`) — swap it for `section.visibleRecords.count` and every collapsed section reads 0, breaking **"a collapsed header still shows its count"**.
  4. `disclosure:` on that same header (`:1413`) — pass `nil` and Done / Failed / Canceled lose the chevron and stop being clickable at all, removing the feature from three of the four sections.
  Two further view-level facts are unpinnable for the same reason and belong in the same list: that the header's button actually calls `onToggleSection`, that the chevron actually rotates, and — new this round — **that the running indicator survives collapse (F1)**, which is a view-level `if` and cannot be pinned by any assertion on the presentation type: a test that the type ignores the collapse state would be tautological, and would not stop a future edit from re-wrapping the indicator in `if isExpanded`. Inventing that test would have made coverage look better without making it better, so it was not written.
  What guards all of this is SONNY-49's manual-test checklist, now four items: item 1 covers (4), item 2 covers (1) and (2), item 3 covers (3), and the new item 4 covers F1. The same enumeration is in the code, on `TasksFoundationView.collapseState`, where an editor will actually meet it. Adding a view-inspection dependency would pin them and is deliberately not done: that is an architectural decision reserved for the user, not a ticket-level one. Recorded so a green suite is never mistaken for full coverage of the feature.
- **Two verified-inaccurate sentences are still in the tree, routed no-action by the coordinator at cycle 2** — recorded here rather than dropped, since a finding that is neither fixed nor written down is a silent backlog. **F4:** both this entry and `docs/sonny-founder-design-decisions.md` say the new chevron reuses the *color* of the two pre-existing System A chevrons; that is true of `CommandCenterView.swift:155`, which sets `SonnyTheme.muted` explicitly, and not of `:282`, which sets no color and inherits `sidebarNavText` from its enclosing `HStack` when enabled. Size, weight and trailing placement are shared by both; only "color" overreaches, and the shipped implementation is unaffected either way. **F5:** `TaskSectionCollapsePresentation.swift:62` justifies `object(forKey:) as? [String]` over `stringArray(forKey:)` "for the same reason the preference rule bans `.bool(forKey:)`" — a false analogy, because `.bool(forKey:)` coerces a missing key to `false` while `stringArray(forKey:)` returns `nil` for anything that is not an array of strings, exactly like the cast. The reviewer proved it: substituting `stringArray` leaves the suite green. The accessor is right; only the reason given is wrong. Both are one-line edits whenever the user wants them.
- **No "collapse all" / "expand all" affordance.** Not asked for; each section is toggled on its own.
- **Collapse state is not shared with the floating widget** — the widget has no status sections, so there is nothing to share.

Behavior added:
- **A workspace's contents are its restriction scope.** `WorkspaceScope` canonicalizes a stored workspace once into app keys, web domains and file roots, and answers a four-valued `ScopeVerdict` per resource. Entries it cannot match — a folder outside `PathWhitelist`, a URL `SafeURL` rejects, a blank app name — become `inertEntries` and are reported rather than dropped.
- **Out-of-scope work escalates to tier 3 and names what it found.** `WorkspaceScopeEvaluator` walks the resolved plan, `PlanScopedResources` classifies what each step touches, and the escalation reason names both the resource and the workspace. Nothing blocks; the user can always allow.
- **A task is bound to a workspace for its lifetime and no longer.** Resolved once after the plan exists and before the first assessment, held across an approval or clarification pause, cleared at every terminal state, and surfaced as a visible, clearable chip.
- **"New task in this workspace" from the workspace card**, arming a binding the next composer dispatch consumes.
- **An `edit_workspace` capability** — add or remove apps, safe URLs, and Desktop/Documents folders — tier 2 to add, tier 3 to remove, with a *different* consent when a removal empties a dimension, because "removing `~/Documents/ClientAlpha`" and "this workspace will no longer restrict file locations at all" are different things to agree to.
- **A workspace detail sheet** showing name, solo/team, task count and all three scope dimensions with every stored entry verbatim; empty dimensions read as *not restricted* with a per-kind sentence; inert entries render visibly as not in effect, carrying the evaluator's own reason; each Remove control states the real removal unit when other rows leave with it.
- **A workspace may list an app the launch catalog cannot open** (SONNY-44), for scope membership only — which is what lets Microsoft Word be inside a workspace's boundary at all.

Behavior preserved (required, no blanket claims):
- **An unscoped task assesses exactly as it did before this branch.** `AgentRunner`'s scope parameter is `.unscoped` *at every call site that means unscoped* — **it has no default, by design** (*corrected by the PR #32 review, cycle 1, F6: this sentence originally said the parameter "defaults to `.unscoped`", which is the opposite of the property the same entry praises below. `grep -rn "scope: TaskWorkspaceScope *=" Sources/` returns nothing; `AgentRunner.swift`'s own comment ends "A default is what makes that failure silent, so there isn't one." A future session must not rely on a default that does not exist*), and `neitherUnscopedNorAnUnconstrainedKindChangesTheAssessment` pins the *whole* assessment — tier, escalations and requirement — not just the tier.
- **A workspace that configures one kind and not another is unchanged on the kind it never configured.** `.unconstrained` produces no escalation and is never relaxation-eligible.
- **Scheduled/unattended runs pass `.unscoped` explicitly**, with the reason at the call site: a stored routine can never name a workspace, there is no user-typed command, and no dispatch named one. The unattended gate's fixed `.approved(.tier2)` is untouched, so nothing this branch mints as tier 3 can run unattended.
- **`open_workspace` still opens exactly what it opened.** Its own plan-derived binding means opening a workspace raises no scope prompt against itself; `theExistingOpenActionIsUnchangedByTheNewCardDispatch` pins the one-click open through the injected seams, with no approval and the card arm dead.
- **`create_workspace` is behaviourally unchanged apart from no longer destroying fields it was not told about** — `WorkspaceStore.save` now merge-preserves `teamType` alongside `fileLocations` (SONNY-43), so "create a workspace called X with Safari" no longer silently demotes a team workspace to solo.
- **`UnattendedTrustAdvisory`'s behaviour is edited not at all** — its entire diff is one call line, one comment and one test argument; its tier-3 threshold, its `try?` and its nil results are byte-identical, and every one of its tests passes unchanged.
- **The evaluator's matching semantics were never re-derived anywhere.** `PlanScopedResources.swift` and `WorkspaceScope.swift` carry zero diff across SONNY-37's commits; `edit_workspace` reuses `WorkspaceScope.appKey`, `WorkspaceScope.normalizedHost` and `PathWhitelist.canonicalURL` rather than copying them, and SONNY-41's sheet asks `verdict(for:)` rather than reaching for keys that are not visible outside `MacAgentCore`.
- **The Command Center card grid, the Tasks region, the Insights workspace breakdown, the widget's own layout and both theme files are untouched by SONNY-41**, verified by diff at each review rather than asserted.
- **Approval copy for every non-scope escalation is unchanged in wording**; only its colour moved off the error token, and both approval surfaces already agreed on the replacement.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**Escalation reasons are questions, not errors — everywhere.** Founder decision (user, 2026-08-06), taken on a two-part question put before any styling was written. The widget's escalation-reasons line moved from `WidgetTheme.errorGlyph` (#FF7474) to `WidgetTheme.secondaryCircular` (**#FF9230**, System B amber), the counterpart to Command Center's `SonnyTheme.warning`. The principle is broader than the pixel: **no escalation is an error** — each one explains why approval is being asked — so "Zip output already exists at …" was wrongly red too, and the token sits on the shared line rather than being conditioned on reason kind. The requirement "must be visually distinguishable from Sonny's error states" was made *checkable* rather than asserted, by enumerating first and subtracting after: `errorGlyph` had exactly three uses, of which the escalation line was the only non-error one; afterwards it is used exclusively by genuine error states, so the property is true by construction of the palette. **The two token systems are not mixed:** Command Center's panel already used `SonnyTheme.warning` (#F2BE00) and was correctly left with zero diff, because a System B token on a System A surface is the mistake this rule exists to prevent.

**The two-notions-of-empty class — three appearances on one branch, and the generalisable rule.** This is the single most valuable thing in this entry. Each time, a second, locally-obvious notion of "empty" was written beside the evaluator's, agreed with it in the common case, and diverged exactly where an inert entry exists:
1. **SONNY-40, first shipped state.** `removalEmptiesTheKind` counted raw surviving strings, so a removal taking a kind's last *working* entry while an inert one survived handed the approver the milder entry-naming consent and un-restricted the dimension anyway — precisely the failure the two-reason requirement exists to prevent.
2. **SONNY-40, cycle 2.** With emptiness fixed, the *escalation trigger* still diffed raw stored strings, so removing an entry that never restricted anything asked for tier-3 approval on a loss that could not occur.
3. **SONNY-41.** The detail sheet derived restricted/not-restricted from `entries.isEmpty` — reintroducing, under a different name and one commit later, the predicate SONNY-40 had just removed, on the surface whose entire job is telling the user whether a dimension restricts. Worse here than there, and inverted from the failure the ticket was written against: the user reads a dimension as restricting when nothing is, and the sheet withholds the one sentence that would say otherwise.
**The rule: ask the evaluator; never re-derive its answer.** `WorkspaceScope` reports `.unconstrained` whenever its *canonical* list is empty, and its own doc comment says that includes the all-inert case. **The reason this keeps recurring is that the wrong version is always the shorter expression** — `after.isEmpty` and `entries.isEmpty` both read naturally and both compile, and a suite whose every fixture has an unrestricted dimension that is *also* an empty one can never tell the two sources apart. The fixture that separates them is a workspace whose three lists are all non-empty and one of which is entirely inert; SONNY-41's `theFootnoteFollowsTheEvaluatorEvenWhenNoListIsEmpty` is that fixture, and it exists only because a mutation battery found the gap after the headline fix had already landed.

**Adding a field to a lifecycle whose clear sites are enumerated in several places, twice in two tickets.** SONNY-38's review filed F2 against `clearInMemoryLocalDataState` for `explicitWorkspaceBinding`; SONNY-39 then added `pendingWorkspaceBinding` and repeated it exactly (F4). The shape: *a new field joins a lifecycle whose clear sites are enumerated in four places, and nothing forces the enumeration to be revisited.* Both are fixed and pinned, and the enumeration is now written out in the function rather than trusted — but the class is the record, not the two instances. **A new binding-like field is not done when it is set and read; it is done when every clear site has been re-enumerated by hand.** The same shape produced SONNY-39's R1 (deleting a workspace left an arm naming it alive, so the chip promised a boundary the run would not apply) — a third instance, reached through a different function.

**The pending-arm lifecycle contract.** A pending card binding **binds exactly one task: the next composer dispatch.** It used to be consumed by *any* `start()`, which meant an armed-but-never-submitted chip was inherited by the next row action — arm "Drafting", get distracted, click Open on "Research", and Research opened under Drafting's boundary and raised a scope prompt naming a workspace the user never mentioned. Now: a composer dispatch consumes it, **every other dispatch kills it**, and either way it dies at the dispatch so it can never reach a second task. `fromComposer: Bool = false` is the safe default **by design, not by convention** — a call site added later that says nothing drops the arm rather than silently scoping itself with it. An explicit `workspaceBinding:` argument still wins over both, keeping the card-beats-free-text precedence a single slot.

**H1 — voice and typed dispatch must be gated by the same terms.** The typed composer is `.disabled(isTaskInFlight)`, which includes a pending clarification; `canUseVoice` had no clarification term. That asymmetry was omission, not a decision anyone made, and it was reachable: during a clarification pause the chip shows the *paused* task's workspace while a live arm is invisible, the card's "New task" button is enabled (both `isRunning` and `isAwaitingApproval` are false), and a voice dispatch then consumes the invisible arm — measured, with the task running scoped to a workspace the chip never named, and the paused task's unanswered clarification silently discarded in the same step. **Ruling: voice gains the clarification term, restoring parity.** The dispatch refuses too, not from belt-and-braces habit but because a transcription already in flight when a clarification arrives would otherwise still land — the guard at the dispatch makes the guarantee independent of that timing. Recorded alternative for a future ticket: voice *answering* a clarification is a feature, and building the gate first does not foreclose it. **The auto-collapse ruling stands, but its safety basis was corrected**: the original argument rested on "an invisible live arm can bind nothing the user does not aim at the composer while seeing the chip," which H1 falsified. The ruling survives on the corrected gates instead — push-to-talk calls `requestWidgetPresentation()` before `beginPushToTalkVoice()`, and `isCollapsible` is false whenever voice is active, so the widget cannot auto-collapse between the hotkey and the consume. No collapse-timer hook was needed; the collapse was never the hole.

**Never-touch lists are read for intent, not letter — three ratifications on this branch.** All three follow one shape: **stated openly rather than slipped in, bounded to the smallest checkable change, ratified by the user, and recorded.** (1) SONNY-37's signature propagation into `UnattendedTrustAdvisory.swift` — a non-defaulted `scope:` parameter refuses to be silent by design, and that file is an executor call site; the discharge was one call line plus one test argument, with `.unscoped` being the semantically correct value rather than merely the compiling one. (2) SONNY-31's copy amendment, the precedent. (3) SONNY-40's one exhaustive-switch arm in `AgentActivityPresentation.swift` (`case .editWorkspace: return "Edit workspace"`) — the branch cannot compile without it and the only alternative is a `default:` clause the conventions forbid for exactly the silent-swallowing reason. **The pattern to reuse: when a never-touch list collides with a compiler requirement or a non-defaulted parameter, the answer is a narrow, checkable discharge condition put to the user — not a quiet edit, and not a `default:`.**

**Stated wireframe exception (SONNY-41).** `13-MainAppWorkspaces.svg` is a card grid only; **no wireframe exists for a workspace detail surface.** The sheet is net-new UI in **System A** — flat, opaque, Inter, zero shadows — and deliberately does *not* inherit the routine-detail view's System-B-inside-System-A treatment, because **liquid glass was tried for workspace surfaces and explicitly reverted as too distracting from card content.** Structurally it follows `TaskLogDetailDialog`, the System A dialog already in that file. Recorded here as a reasoned exception per CLAUDE.md's rule, not silent drift; the card grid behind it is visually unchanged.

**Process pitfall: a mutation battery reverts `Sources/` with `git checkout`, so it must only ever run against a committed tree.** Running one over uncommitted work during SONNY-40 **destroyed a round of fixes that then had to be redone.** The battery is worth its cost — it found the two-notions-of-empty class, the `restricts(.webDomain)` blind spot, SONNY-41's task-count pluralisation and the badge-write boundary gap, none of which reading found — but its revert step is indiscriminate. Commit first, every time.

**Entry identity is not the evaluator's resource matching.** `verdict(for:)` answers "does this resource fall inside the boundary" — folder *containment* and a dot-suffix host match. That is the wrong question for "which stored entry does this removal name": under it, "remove `~/Documents/ClientAlpha`" would delete a stored `~/Documents`. Removal matching is *equality* of the same canonical forms, reused rather than re-derived. URLs deliberately carry two keys: removal matches by **host** (so a removal that left the host in scope would change no boundary at all), while addition dedupes by the whole URL (two pages on one host legitimately both belong). SONNY-41's sheet, which cannot see those key functions, recovers the same equality by asking the evaluator **twice, symmetrically** — a one-way probe would group a parent folder with its child, and symmetry turns those deliberately asymmetric rules back into equality.

**Removals are derived from the outcome, never from the request.** A request-derived list would call "remove Safari, add Safari" a loss, escalate for nothing, and make the answer depend on whether removals or additions applied first. What the user loses is a property of the outcome, so it is read from the outcome.

**A plan may edit one workspace only once.** `AgentRunner` gates once up front and `executeChain` never re-gates, so a second edit of the same workspace is assessed against a store the first has not yet written to — two "one of several" consents could between them empty a dimension with neither saying so. The rule lives in `resolveDefaultOutputs`, the one hook handed the whole plan; a per-segment count structurally cannot see the shape it needs to reject. Editing two *different* workspaces is allowed, because they share no record and each assessment is correct in isolation.

**`edit_workspace` is forbidden inside routines.** The capability's own new operation opened the hole: removal escalates to tier 3, which an unattended run structurally cannot satisfy, but *addition* stays tier 2, which it can — so a scheduled routine could have widened a workspace's restriction scope with nobody present. `PlanScopedResources` refuses a `default:` clause precisely so a new operation cannot land unclassified, but a `Set` has no such guard.

Known limitations / deferred scope:
- **No relaxation ships here, by design.** In-scope tier 2 auto-running and in-scope tier 3 dropping to lightweight confirmation are row C's. Row B computes the verdict, stores it on the assessment, and **uses it only to escalate.** Row C inherits a typed input plus the two constraints now written into spec §11.2.
- **SONNY-40 residual R1 (records, low).** `removalEmptiesTheKind`'s doc comment argues its own equivalence proof over *canonical* lists while the conjunct it retired was phrased over `removed`, a list derived through `entryKey` — a different function that can collide across the inert/valid boundary. The conclusion (reduce to two terms) is right; only the stated reason reasons over the wrong domain. A measured counterexample is on the ticket.
- **SONNY-40 residual R2 (pre-existing, low, unreachable through the product).** The same collision is a real escalation gap — a removal that empties a kind can run at tier 2 when an inert stored entry's `entryKey` collides with the removed working entry's. Identical at the previous head, so this round neither introduced nor widened it, and it needs a hand-edited or pre-validation store file to reach.
- **SONNY-41 residual: the inert-sibling shared-key note gap (bounded, low).** The sheet's symmetric probe gates on `verdict(for:)`, which is `.unconstrained` for a scope built from an inert entry, so two inert entries never group; the adapter's removal key gates on neither the whitelist nor `SafeURL`, so two inert entries that canonicalise alike *do* share one. Removing either takes both while the note names nothing. **The direction is under-report, never over-report** — the note can never name an entry that survives — it is confined to rows that now visibly read "Not in effect", so no boundary can be lost, and reaching it needs a hand-edited store with two near-duplicate inert entries. Recorded rather than fixed.
- **SONNY-62 — the tier-equal drift, and row C's input.** An approval granted for one tier-3 reason silently covers a *different* tier-3 reason arising before execution: the stale-approval guard re-assesses fresh but compares tiers only, and two different tier-3 causes compare equal. Observed in a real run during SONNY-38's manual pass — the user consented to a scope exception and the run then overwrote a file that had appeared in the meantime, without the replace escalation ever surfacing. **Pre-existing** (the guard predates row B, and `AgentRunner` gating is on this branch's never-touch lists) but **materially more reachable now**, because out-of-scope escalations mint tier-3 prompts routinely where before they were rare. Filed untriaged, and flagged as row C input either way.
- **Planner-prompt routine rule (pre-existing, deliberately not widened).** The system prompt's routine rule names `save_routine`, `run_routine`, `clarify` and `unsupported` as forbidden inside `routineSteps`; it already omitted `create_workspace` and `open_workspace` before this branch and now omits `edit_workspace` too. Enforcement is at the store and the save capability, so this is a prompt-quality gap rather than a hole. Not widened here on purpose: correcting it would edit a golden-pinned prompt for a problem this branch did not create.
- **Two `edit_workspace` steps separated by a step of another operation still segment apart.** The pure case is refused outright, which is the reachable shape. Not fixed because the only two routes are an executor special-case the contract forbids or per-segment re-gating the conventions forbid; it is a pre-existing property of gate-once assessment that `create_workspace` and `save_routine` share.
- **SONNY-43 stays open as its own tracking ticket and closes at merge, citing `795a19a`**, per its 2026-08-06 ratification note.
- **Product tickets the manual passes generated, all untriaged and none touching this branch:** SONNY-64 (direct picker UX plus pre-built-plan dispatch, removing the composer round-trip), SONNY-65 (app icons beside names in the sheet's app rows), SONNY-66 (a mechanism decision for expanding the app catalog beyond the hardcoded twelve), and a row-C origin-signal input recorded on SONNY-13 — with the guard rails already attached to it: the origin signal must be unforgeable from the planner side (an enum set only by UI call sites, the shape SONNY-39's `fromComposer` already uses), `effectiveTier` stays honest, and the unattended path is unaffected.
- **View-level rendering remains unpinnable**, as everywhere in this repo — no SwiftUI view-inspection harness. All presentation logic was moved into pure tested functions; what the view *renders* is covered by each ticket's manual items, all of which the user executed.

Open questions (required, write "none" if true):
- **Should a scheduled run's unattended pre-check assess with the run's real scope?** Flagged by SONNY-37 and deliberately not resolved: answering "yes" would make `UnattendedTrustAdvisory`'s pre-check disagree with its own docstring, which already warns that a clean result is not a promise the routine will run. Not live in any current contract; belongs to whoever owns the unattended path. **Cost amended in place 2026-08-13 (SONNY-100, founder-ratified as part of that ticket — the question stays open; only its weight is corrected):** after row C, answering "yes" has a second, much larger consequence that was not on the table when this was parked — it would make in-scope tier-2 steps auto-run unattended, without the per-routine trust opt-in, by removing one of the two independent call-site choices (`source: .instantResolver`, `scope: .unscoped`) that keep the unattended path outside both relaxation grants (row C's I6, a pinned property with a named test, not a type-level guarantee).
- **Should adding to scope deserve more than a lightweight confirmation once relaxation exists?** — **Answered by row C (SONNY-98), 2026-08-13.** The reasoning as raised, kept: row B rejected escalating on *widening* on a row-B cost argument — the user typed the command asking for it — and once relaxation is live, an ungated tier-2 edit that adds `~/Documents` converts a large share of the filesystem into relaxation-eligible territory in one un-escalated step; Gate 1 answers *which verdicts qualify*, not whether creating a qualifying verdict should itself be gated. The answer: the origin grant never covers a boundary-changing edit, and adding a `PathWhitelist` root itself escalates to tier 3 with a consequence-naming reason. See `docs/sonny-founder-design-decisions.md` → "Approval relaxation (roadmap row C)" and the row-C branch entry below.

Next branch: `feature/approval-relaxation-structural` (row C), per the roadmap above — now unblocked, since its stated justification was restriction scoping existing first. It inherits `CapabilityRiskAssessment.scopeVerdict` as a typed input rather than re-deriving scope, the three constraints recorded on row C's roadmap line and now in spec §11.2, and the two open questions above.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**The trust decision is derived from the plan, through the store's own lookup — never from a call site.** `runRoutineWidget` holds the real `StoredRoutine` and deliberately throws it away (it round-trips through the same text command a user would type), and the planner path only ever holds a `routineName` string. So `manualRoutineTrustDecision(for:)` re-derives the routine from the plan's single `run_routine` step via `routineStore.routine(named:)` — the identical normalized (case/diacritic-insensitive) lookup `RunRoutineCapabilityAdapter.routineRunSpec` performs at execute time, so the routine the check reads and the routine that runs cannot resolve differently. Every unresolvable case — unknown name, nameless step, unreadable store — fails closed to `.notRequested`: a trust check that cannot complete relaxes nothing.

**The grant covers exactly the canonical single-step run-routine plan.** A planner-built plan wrapping `run_routine` beside any other step keeps the full prompt: those steps were never what the user marked trusted. The planner is not injectable at the view-model level, so this shape rule is pinned by calling the (internal-not-private, for exactly this reason) decision function directly.

**The view-model tier comparison is a courtesy pre-check; the enforcement is `AgentRunner`'s structural gate — and the mutation battery proved it.** Mutant M4 (comparison always-true) left all 92 ScheduledRoutineRunTests+ProductShellTests green *with correct user-visible behavior*: the trusted tier-3 run proceeded into `execute`, the gate threw, and the new drift catch re-armed the prompt. The split above still stands — user-visible behavior under M4 was correct, verified by the reviewer two ways — but the divergence is now test-observable rather than survivable.*

**The drift catch is deterministically unreachable in-process, and its body is proven by the mutant, not by a test.** Between `performStart`'s assessment and `execute`'s re-assessment there is no main-actor suspension point, so no test can interleave a store rewrite there (ProductShellTests' re-arm test exploits the *approval pause* window, which the trusted path removes). The window is real for external state (a file appearing on disk mid-flight), so the catch stays; M4's run exercised its entire body on the real path.

**Trust remains schedule-scoped — a deliberate consequence of "no new persisted state."** `unattendedTrusted` lives on `RoutineSchedule` (a persisted coding key; the name predates the widening and keeps its old spelling), the toggle renders only when a schedule exists, and `setRoutineUnattendedTrust` no-ops without one. A never-scheduled routine therefore cannot be trusted and always prompts.

**Mutation-battery pattern hygiene: count before you mutate.** M1's first pattern (`routine.schedule?.unattendedTrusted == true else {`) matched twice — the helper *and* `checkScheduledRoutines`' scheduled-path guard — and would have mutated the never-touch scheduled gate; the mutate script's occurrence-count guard refused it, and the re-anchored pattern killed cleanly (17 issues across both suites). M5 and M6 are absent from the numbering by design, not omission: M5 (deleting the drift catch) was designed and dropped because no in-process test can reach the catch — there is no main-actor suspension point between the assessment and `execute`'s re-assessment for a test to interleave into — and M6 (inverting the trust-field read) was dropped as behaviorally bracketed by the M1/M2 pair, which mutate the same condition from both directions. Behavior added:
- **The verdict is about the app that will actually be switched to.** The adapter's new `resolveDefaultOutputs` hook runs in the resolve phase all three executor gates (`prepare`, `assessRisk`, `execute`) pass through first, resolves `RunningAppMatcher.bestMatch` exactly once, and pins the winner's display name and bundle identifier into the step. Classification reads the pin as `ScopedResource.resolvedApp`, matched bundle-identifier-first with a name fallback that deliberately never catalog-resolves — an app that merely *calls itself* "Chrome" cannot spend the cataloged Chrome's membership.
- **Execution activates the pin or fails naming it.** A pinned step is looked up by exact bundle identifier; if the app quit, execution throws `noMatchingRunningApp` with the pinned name — it never re-fuzzy-matches the query onto something the assessment never scored.
- **The consent surfaces name the resolved app.** Escalation reasons and the approval's involved-resource line carry the resolved display name ("Xcode is not part of the Writing workspace."), never the query string and never a bundle identifier.

Behavior preserved (required, no blanket claims):
- **An unpinned step classifies, previews, and executes exactly as before.** The raw-name classification branch is byte-identical, the adapter's `bestMatch` path survives for direct callers, and the classification-table test plus `switchRunningAppFallsBackToTheSearchQueryWhenNoAppNameIsGiven` pass unchanged — the fail-closed direction: a query that never resolved earns nothing a resolved app would have to spend.
- **The unresolvable-query failure surface is identical**: the same `noMatchingRunningApp(query)` the adapter's preview used to throw from inside `prepare`, thrown by the same `prepare` call, now from the resolve phase — earlier and once, with no pin left behind.
- **Every other operation's resolve phase is untouched** — the new block is additive, shaped exactly like the seven existing ones *(count corrected by the PR #35 review, cycle 1, F2: originally "six"; `git show c46bf89:Sources/MacAgentCore/AgentActionExecutor.swift | grep -c '.resolveDefaultOutputs(in: resolvedPlan'` → 7 — zip, docx, write-markdown, web-to-markdown, local-draft, shortcut, edit-workspace — the count-first-then-write rule applied after the fact)*.
- **Tier defaults, `AgentRunner` gating, the evaluator's web/file matching, `.app` matching for every other operation, and the instant resolver's plan construction: zero diff.**
- **The pre-existing adapter test passes unchanged** (`runningAppSwitchUsesTierOneRunnerPathWithoutCatalogAllowlist`): the partial query "Not" still previews and activates Notion — now via the pin rather than a second resolution.
- **One deliberate verdict-flip class, in both directions, and it is the ticket's point**: a query that catalog-resolves to a listed app while the running match is a different app flips false-`.inScope` → truthful-`.outOfScope` (new prompt, correct); a partial query resolving to the listed running app flips false-`.outOfScope` → truthful-`.inScope` (a prompt disappears — a *correction of a false escalation*, not a relaxation mechanism: row B still relaxes nothing on `.inScope`, and the flip is earned by binding the verdict to the real resource, never by loosening a comparison).

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**Pin once, first resolver wins — and the idempotency is load-bearing, not hygiene.** The resolve phase runs at every gate, so a hook that re-resolved would re-open the exact assessment-versus-execution divergence the pin closes, at the gate boundary where it is least visible. The pin-once guard is what makes "the resolution the approval classified" and "the identity execution activates" the same value by construction. The contract's required definition of behavior-when-resolution-would-change falls out: it cannot change — the pin is immutable after `prepare`; the one residual (the pinned app quitting mid-run) fails closed with the pinned app's name, pinned by `executionActivatesThePinOrFailsClosedWhenThePinnedAppQuit` with a deliberately tempting decoy (an app that would best-match the query) running.

**The anti-imposter rule: a resolved app's name half never catalog-resolves.** `verdict(for: .resolvedApp)` matches `bundle:` first and falls back to `nameFallbackKey(displayName)` only — running `appKey` on the display name would catalog-resolve "Chrome" to the real Chrome's bundle key and hand any app using that display name the workspace membership the user granted to the cataloged app. The name fallback therefore only ever matches stored entries the catalog itself could not resolve, for which name identity is all anyone has. `appKey`'s two constructors were split into shared `bundleKey`/`nameFallbackKey` helpers so the key literals exist once — a drifted prefix would silently unmatch every stored entry of that half.

**`switch_running_app` is structurally single-sourced, which is what makes the pin total.** *(Amended 2026-08-09 by the `feature/planner-vocabulary-routing` branch, at PR #39's cycle-1 review, F5 — the sanctioned in-place pattern this paragraph already uses below. **Two of the three clauses that follow are no longer true.** SONNY-68 removed the operation from `plannerVisibleCases`, so it is in the planner's schema and is no longer constructed only by the instant resolver; the decode-layer block on the pin fields is untouched and still holds, and so does "routines cannot carry it through any product path" — but now because `StoredRoutine.forbiddenStepOperations` refuses it rather than because the planner has no word for it. The pin is still total, for a reason this paragraph did not have to state: a planner-emitted step arrives unpinned and is pinned once at the resolve phase like any other, and the routine ban is what keeps the nested per-gate path — the one with no shared prepared plan — out of reach. See that branch's entry at this file's end.)* The operation is excluded from the planner's JSON schema (`AgentOperation.plannerVisibleCases`), blocked again at the decode layer (`AgentPlanDecoder.stepKeys` omits both pin fields, enforced recursively through `routineSteps`), and constructed only by the instant resolver, single-step; routines cannot carry it through any product path. The recorded corner — a store-tampered routine carrying one (the `RoutineStore.save`-validates-nothing class, PR #28 F5) — has **two variants, and the entry originally enumerated only the milder one** *(completed by the PR #35 review, cycle 1, F1 — the repo's own enumerate-before-you-subtract rule, applied to this paragraph)*: (a) an **unpinned** tampered step resolves per nested gate independently, with no shared prepared plan to pin through; (b) a tampered step with the pin fields **pre-set** is the opposite — the pin-once guard honors the stored pin identically and confidently at every gate, so no cross-gate divergence ever surfaces it. Sharpest sub-case: with a workspace listing an uncataloged app entry (a `name:` key), a tampered `resolvedAppName` matching that entry plus a foreign `resolvedBundleIdentifier` earns `.inScope` silently, renders the display name on the consent line, and activates the other app by exact lookup. The class is unchanged: tamper-only, behind the encrypted store, the same recorded PR #28 F5 class — pre-SONNY-58 tampering could already lie via `appName`, so reachability is not regressed; the new fields make the tampered lie cleaner (the attacker picks the activated bundle id directly, and the consent name and activated app split perfectly). Hardening (strip or reject pre-set pins at routine-store load) is deliberately not this branch's scope — filed as a discovery ticket per step 5, coordinator-adjudicated.

**The truthful-flip constraint, stated for row C.** This ticket makes verdicts more truthful, never more permissive: both flip directions above are the same correction (bind the verdict to the resolved resource), and the disappearing-prompt direction is justified *only* by that binding. Row C consumes `.inScope` as relaxation input; what this branch guarantees it is that a `switch_running_app` `.inScope` was earned by the app execution will actually activate.

**Mutation battery: 8 designed, 8 killed, against the committed tree at `ffaeeb7`, reverted per mutant** (filter: the two touched suites, 69 tests; every mutant compiled and ran the full pair, exit 1). M1 classifier-ignores-pin → killed by the headline, partial-query, and classification tests; M2 executor-never-pins → killed by four tests including both execution pins; M3 pin-once-idempotency-dropped → killed by the re-resolve and quit tests; M4 execution-falls-back-to-fuzzy-rematch → killed by the quit test, whose running decoy (an app that would best-match the query) exists for exactly that mutant; M5 name-half-catalog-resolves → killed by the imposter test alone, likewise its purpose-built killer; M6 bundle-half-dropped → killed by the bundle-first and partial-query tests; M7 value-renders-bundle-identifier → killed by the rendering and headline tests; M8 approval-line-ignores-pin → killed by the headline's approval-copy assertion.

Known limitations / deferred scope:
- **The unpinned classification and execution paths remain**, reachable only by direct adapter/classifier callers (tests) and the tampered-routine corner above — both keep pre-SONNY-58 behavior, which is the fail-closed direction.
- **The pin freezes resolution at prepare time by design.** A user who approves a tier-3 escalation and takes long enough that the pinned app quits gets a failure naming that app rather than a fresh match — decided over re-resolving, because a silent re-match is the bug this ticket exists to remove.

**The mandate (founder, on SONNY-69, 2026-08-08).** The experiment graduates from throwaway spike to v1-integration input; reshaping the roadmap in its service is intended, not incidental. **The thirteen ratified decisions, compressed (full text: plan §E).** Production A/B for the planner, OpenAI default until a benchmark passes (E1); the open-weights planner lands behind a formalized provider-agnostic router, not a second hardcoded `performStart` branch (E2); the vision loop is one capability (E3) that pauses mid-session only on consequential actions — a lightweight confirmation for anything affecting another person, explicit approval for anything destructive (E4); vision is auto-*proposed* when the planner falls short — no separate "enable vision" step, but one up-front approval of the envelope before anything fires, so D5(a)'s trigger with D5(b)'s consent rather than either option as written (E5); made safe by per-app vision-control consent with terminals never controllable (E6, which also resolves SONNY-66's mechanism as per-app consent); unattended vision never (E7); the roadmap splits — screen-*seeing* + transparency infra pulled forward, screen-*acting* stays as rescoped Power Mode (E8); a two-mode model — low-friction Normal (post-hoc sent-data log, no pre-send screenshot) and a global Safe mode (asks before every task, shows every screenshot pre-send), with the "data leaves device" label relocated to Safe mode only (E9, reshaping SONNY-32); auto-blur secrets before sending and never obey on-screen instruction text (E9); screenshots to Cerebras no-retention only, never Google's free tier (E10); a benchmark for both models gating any default change, its two halves owned separately by SONNY-70 (vision) and SONNY-72 (planner) (E11); cleanup-first sequencing (E12); the spike reworked-not-merged and last (E13).

**The safety-critical unknown, named so it is not a surprise later.** E4's "pause only on consequential actions" requires the vision model to recognize, *before* it clicks, that a button sends a message or deletes something — a runtime judgment that can be wrong both ways (miss a real Send, or over-nag). Its accuracy is the single number **SONNY-70** — the vision half of E11's benchmark: screenshot-reading + action-coordinate accuracy over a labeled offline fixture set — must establish; "feels accurate" is not a basis for shipping this gate. SONNY-70 is therefore a hard gate on the whole **action** half, not a metric to collect afterward: no vision-action ships until its numbers clear. **E11's two halves have separate owners and neither absorbs the other** (corrected by PR #37's review, F3 — this entry originally called SONNY-70 a "two-model" benchmark and hung the planner-default gate on it too). SONNY-70 is deliberately vision-only; "no multi-model leaderboard" is its own non-goal, and it produces no plan-quality number, so it structurally cannot discharge E1's "never flip the default to Cerebras without proof." That gate is **SONNY-72** (filed by the fix round, Backlog, untriaged): plan-quality parity, structured-output rejection rate with a live nullable-union re-check, end-to-end latency, and the reliability envelope — plan §A5's four numbers, seeded by SONNY-69's own never-run acceptance criteria, and the place §D11's unanswered "who runs it, against which command set?" now gets settled. Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**The ticket's stated trigger cannot be observed at the moment it would be needed, and implementing it literally would have shipped a dead branch.** SONNY-59 and SONNY-45 both describe the condition as "`contextSource == .finderSelection` **and no input path was supplied**", adding that the classifier knows both at assessment time. It does not. The only production path into `PlanScopedResources.classification` is `AgentActionExecutor.assessRisk` -> `scopeFindings` -> `WorkspaceScopeEvaluator.evaluate`, and `assessRisk`'s first statement is `resolveDefaultOutputs`, which runs `FinderSelectionResolver.pinningSelectedDirectoryInput` and writes the resolved folder into `inputPath` on every matching step. `selectedDirectoryPath` either returns a path or throws, so there is no third outcome that reaches classification with `inputPath` still empty — a populated `inputPath` is evidence the selection **was** read, not evidence it was not. The two-condition form is therefore unfalsifiable-looking and inert: it fires on no real plan while passing every classifier test written from an unresolved step, because such tests construct steps the resolve phase never touched. The classifier keys on `contextSource` alone; the residual over-report (a step reaching classification with both a real `inputPath` and `contextSource`, where the resolver returns the supplied path and never talks to Finder) is the direction this file already takes for Word, and its reachable form is the cross-step pooled shape bounded under "Known limitations" below — *not* a per-step planner violation, which is what the first version of this entry wrongly claimed excluded it. **This is recorded as the pitfall rather than the fix because the general lesson is the trap, not this instance: a classifier condition written against the plan as the planner emits it, evaluated against the plan as the gates see it, is a branch that reads as coverage and is not.** The measurement is in the mutation battery below — the literal reading is mutant M4, and the executor-level test reports it as `escalations → []`, `effectiveTier → .tier2`, `scopeVerdict → .inScope`.

**`convert_docx_to_pdf` is in scope for this ticket even though its context paragraph names only three operations.** The founder decision authorizes "the selection-driven paths", not an operation list, and `DocxConversionCapabilityAdapter` pins `[.scanDocx, .convertDocxToPDF]` and falls back to `convertStep?.contextSource` in its own `spec` — so a convert step is a genuine selection reader, including alone, since a plan carrying only that operation still routes to that adapter through `AgentActionExecutor.workflow(for:)`. Enumerating before subtracting is what surfaced it: the fourth operation is invisible if the three named in the ticket are taken as the population. Note this is a different resource from SONNY-45 item 2's "RELAX on `convert_docx_to_pdf`", which is about Word's conditionality and remains untouched.

**The `open_generated_artifact` warning three cases below is about a different site, and this change is on the other side of its own rule.** That comment (SONNY-37's F4 discharge, landed in SONNY-40) records that the death of the unlistability argument is *not* licence to report the Launch-Services handler. The rule that survives there is drives-versus-resolves: an app the capability drives by name is a resource; an app the system resolves for a file already inside the boundary is not. `FinderSelectionResolver` drives Finder by name over Apple Events, which is the reported side of that exact rule — the same rule the branch-B plan states at `docs/sonny-branch-b-plan.md:204` while its own resource table (lines 220-221) lists scan/zip/docx as file-only. That table is the stale artifact this branch corrects in code; it is left unedited because branch B's plan is a frozen historical planning document, and this entry is the durable record of the correction.

**Mutation battery: 5 designed, 5 killed, against the committed tree at `02732dc`, reverted per mutant** (the full flagged suite per mutant, each reporting `Test run with 727 tests in 56 suites failed`; the restored tree re-ran green at 727 / 56, exit 0). M1 Finder dropped from the scan/zip/docx case → killed by 5 tests, 15 issues, including the executor escalation test and the 31-case table; M2 Finder dropped from `convert_docx_to_pdf` only → killed by 2 tests (the table and the four-operation classifier test), proving the fourth operation is covered independently rather than by association; M3 Finder reported unconditionally → killed by the plain-form half of the classifier test and by the mixed-plan attribution test (`["scan", "zip"]` vs `["scan"]`), which is what stops the fix from escalating every explicitly-named folder; M4 the ticket's literal two-condition reading → killed by 4 tests, 16 issues, the executor-level test showing the dead branch directly; M5 selection-driven steps additionally marked opaque → killed by 5 tests, including the counter-test's `.inScope` roll-up and the table's opacity assertion. **M5's issue count is construction-dependent and two measurements exist**: 5 tests / **9 issues** as run by this session at `02732dc`, which marked only the `.scanSelectLargestFiles, .createZip, .scanDocx` case opaque, and 5 tests / **11 issues** as reproduced by PR #38's cycle-1 review at `4adf94a` (docs-only delta, so the same code tree), which marked the `.convertDocxToPDF` case opaque as well and therefore tripped two extra table assertions. Same five killing tests, same kill; the delta is the mutant, not the coverage. Recorded rather than reconciled to one number because an issue count without its mutant text is not reproducible — the tests killed are the durable measurement.

Known limitations / deferred scope:
- **The over-report is accepted, not fixed — and its true class is cross-step, not the per-step shape first recorded here.** Any step reaching classification with both `contextSource` and a non-empty `inputPath` names Finder even when `selectedDirectoryPath` returned the supplied path and never contacted Finder. The reachable form is produced by pooling, not by a malformed step: `pinningSelectedDirectoryInput` takes `primary` from the first non-empty `inputPath` among the plan's matching steps and `contextSource` from the first non-nil among them, *independently*, so a scan carrying an explicit path with no `contextSource` beside a zip carrying `contextSource` with no path resolves from the scan's path with zero Finder contact, back-fills it into the zip, and the zip is reported as driving Finder. Both steps individually satisfy `OpenAIPlanner.swift:162`. **The first version of this entry bounded the residual with "a plan shape the planner is instructed not to produce" — that bound was unsound**, because per-step planner compliance says nothing about a cross-step pool; PR #38's cycle-1 review executed the shape (`finderReads=0`, tier 3, `.outOfScope`) and the correction is recorded here rather than quietly replaced. What genuinely bounds the cost is direction: always an extra escalation, never a silent blessing or an under-report, so no workspace boundary can be widened by it. Exactness belongs to the resolver, the only place that knows whether Finder was contacted — filed as **SONNY-73** (Backlog, untriaged), which also has to decide whether clearing `contextSource` or pinning a provenance marker (SONNY-58's pattern) is right, since the second changes what an *unresolved* plan classifies as.
- **Attribution in a mixed plan is per declaring step, not per plan.** `pinningSelectedDirectoryInput` reads the selection once for the whole plan and pins every matching step, so in a plan where only one step carries `contextSource` that step is the one naming Finder. Where the selection really was read, this is attribution only — the plan-level roll-up is a maximum, so the verdict is identical and only the finding's `stepID` differs from a plan-scoped attribution. **It is not attribution only in the pooled shape above**: there the escalation has no Finder read behind it at all, which is SONNY-73's subject, not this one's. Pinned deliberately by `aMixedSelectionDrivenPlanNamesFinderOnceOnTheStepThatDeclaresIt`.
- **Prepending Finder can displace a later resource from the approval message, and that is pre-existing design, not a regression.** `scopeEscalations` dedupes in first-seen order and truncates at `prefix(3)` (`AgentActionExecutor.swift:433-439`), so on a plan with four or more distinct out-of-scope resources a previously-named one can now fall outside the list. No verdict and no tier changes — only which three reasons the prompt spells out — and the cap is deliberate, documented at its own definition, and already covered by `repeatedAndSurplusOutOfScopeResourcesAreDeduplicatedAndCapped`. Recorded so the preserved-behavior list above is exact; no action taken. (Raised as L3 by PR #38's cycle-1 review, which requested no change.)
- **`docs/sonny-branch-b-plan.md`'s resource table (lines 220-221) now under-describes the shipped classifier.** Left as-is per the frozen-historical-document rule above; this entry is the correction of record.

Behavior added:
- **A switch phrasing that names a workspace resolves to a switch, scoped to that workspace.** "switch to code in the workspace Switch" and its three recorded siblings now instant-resolve to `switch_running_app` carrying only the app name, while the clause continues to bind the task's workspace through `WorkspaceTaskTagging` — so SONNY-58's verdict binding decides the consent from the app that will actually be activated. In scope it is tier 1 and silent; out of scope it is a tier-3 approval naming the resolved app. **This is the first time the scoped switch is reachable from command text at all**: SONNY-58's own manual pass had to be restaged through SONNY-39's card arm because every command-text phrasing fell through to a planner that could not express the intent.

- **"in my X workspace" binds a workspace.** The free-text recognizer previously matched only "in [the|my] workspace X", so the fourth recorded misroute named a workspace Sonny never saw. Escalation-only in every direction: an unscoped task escalates for no boundary at all, and a scoped one only escalates when a resource sits outside it.
- **A typed full stop no longer strands itself in the query.** Edge punctuation comes off the candidate on both paths, so "switch to code in the workspace Switch." activates Code rather than failing to find `code .`. Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**The clause was never noise, and treating it as noise would have swapped a loud bug for a quiet one.** The obvious repair — strip "in the workspace X" so the app name fits under the three-word ceiling — is only safe because that same phrase is what `WorkspaceTaskTagging.freeTextWorkspaceName` feeds to `AgentViewModel.resolveTaskScope`, for the instant-resolver branch as much as the planner branch. Had the resolver subtracted a phrase nothing else consumed, a user naming a workspace would have got an unscoped run and no sign of it. **The invariant the fix is built on, and the one to keep if this code is touched again: the resolver removes from the app query exactly the clause that binds the task's scope — one recognizer, two consumers.** It is what forced the second word order into scope; recognizing "in my X workspace" was not opportunistic tidying but the only way to make the invariant true for all four recorded commands.

**A negative that only one of two readers can see is not a boundary, it is a coincidence.** Both tickets are the same defect in different directions — SONNY-68's operation was invisible to the planner while the resolver was assumed to cover it, SONNY-48's was permitted by the routine validator while the planner had no word for it — and in both cases the disagreement was invisible from either side alone. The exclusion list and the empty-`plannerTools` adapters happened to name the same six operations at `48d0150` with nothing requiring it. `PlannerBoundaryTests.plannerExclusionsAgreeWithEmptyToolAdaptersAndWithInstantResolverCoverage` now asserts all three views — excluded from the schema, no planner tool, reachable through the instant resolver — as one set, and drives the third leg from real resolver commands rather than a list, so a resolver change that closes a front door fails there. This is §A4's "add the missing pin", and it is the piece that makes the next SONNY-48-shaped question a decision instead of a discovery.

**Making an operation planner-visible makes it routine-nestable, and the nested path has no shared prepared plan.** The schema builds `routineSteps` from the same `plannerVisibleCases` enum as top-level steps, so the two questions cannot be answered separately. `RunRoutineCapabilityAdapter` calls `routineRunSpec` again from `preview`, `assessRisk` and `execute`, rebuilding the nested plan from the store each time, and each rebuild re-runs `resolveDefaultOutputs` on a fresh unpinned plan — so a nested `switch_running_app` step would be resolved and pinned twice, independently, reopening the assessment-versus-execution divergence SONNY-58 closed. At the top level that cannot happen because `AgentRunner` threads one `preparedRun.plan` through both gates, which is precisely what makes SONNY-58's pin total. `.switchRunningApp` therefore joined `forbiddenStepOperations` — preserving today's reachability exactly (routines could not carry it through any product path before either) and following the existing planner-visible-but-routine-forbidden shape that `create_workspace`, `edit_workspace` and `open_workspace` already have. **The general rule for the next operation that leaves the exclusion list: decide the nested question at the same time, or the schema decides it for you.**

**`.saveSnippet` and `.expandSnippet` are asymmetric on purpose, and the asymmetry is now written down at both ends.** Saving is an automation primitive with a scheduled-run story already built for it; expansion's `execute` returns the snippet text as the run summary and types it nowhere, so a routine-nested expansion produces text with no consumer. Symmetry would have bought prompt surface and no user story. Recorded on the expansion adapter's empty `plannerTools`, on `plannerVisibleCases`, on `forbiddenStepOperations`, and asserted by `snippetExpansionIsStillNotSomethingThePlannerCanAskFor` — four places, because the ticket's actual complaint was that the emptiness read as an omission from every one of them.

**Subtracting a matched phrase from folded text needs an index map, not a second regex.** `normalized(_:)` folds a whole string and gives no way back to the caller's characters, so a range found in the folded copy cannot be cut out of the original — and lowercasing the survivor would have put the wrong words in the summary the user reads. `FoldedText` folds character by character while recording each folded character's source index, and folds the pattern side through the same function, so the two sides of a comparison cannot fold differently. The alternative considered and rejected was a separate literal search in the resolver: that is a second recognizer, and two recognizers of the same phrase are how the resolver and the scope binder would drift apart again.

**A guard is an ordering contract, and moving work in front of one silently repeals part of it.** The first version of this branch narrowed the switch candidate — clause, then leading article, then a trailing " app" — and only then handed it to `looksLikeRunningAppName`. Two of that guard's eight leading stop words are `the` and `my`, which are also the two articles the trim removed, so on this path those rejections stopped existing. Nothing failed: the guard still had six stop words, a word ceiling and a "mode" rule, the code comment said "neither trim touches the guard's own rejections", and the example it picked to prove that was one of the cases still working. What the two dead words were protecting turned out to be **workspace-opening phrasings** — "switch to my Research workspace", "switch to the workspace Switch" — which reached the planner's `open_workspace` rule at `48d0150` and were captured as doomed app queries after the change; and because the new prompt rule as first worded also told the planner never to turn a switch or focus request into `open_workspace`, the same intent was closed at both ends by two edits that each looked local. **The lesson generalises past this function: when you insert a normalisation ahead of a predicate, the predicate's rejection set is part of the contract, and the only honest way to keep it is to enumerate the rejections and measure each one at the base commit.** That is what the base-parity table in `SwitchInWorkspaceRoutingTests` now is — all eight stop words, the ceiling and the "mode" rule, each with its `48d0150` outcome recorded beside it. The shipped mechanism makes the contract structural rather than disciplined: with no clause recognised the candidate is the remainder, untouched, so the guard cannot be partially repealed at all; the one normalisation that remains is gated on a clause and is a *naming form* — `[the|my] NAME app`, where the trailing noun is what declares the phrase names an app — rather than a rule about articles. (PR #39 review, cycle 1, F1.)

**A test whose name says "unchanged" is a claim about the base commit, and it has to be measured there.** `theExistingResolverBehaviourIsUnchangedBy…` asserted that "switch to the Notes app" resolves to `Notes`; at `48d0150` that command returned `nil`. The assertion was true of the head and false as a statement about preservation, and it read to any future reader as evidence the widening was a no-op. Preserved-behaviour tests in this branch now carry the base measurement per case and assert only cases that really are unchanged; everything the branch added has its own named test. Same class as the SONNY-58 entry correction this repo already ran once — a claim that reads as verification of old behaviour when it is really an assertion of new. (PR #39 review, cycle 1, F2.)

**A mutant that survives is either a coverage hole or a bad mutant, and the difference is worth one more run.** The cycle-2 battery's M22 replaced `FoldedText`'s index map with a naive one-entry-per-character version and **survived** the multi-character-fold test written in the same round. The test was the problem, not the coverage bar: every expansion in it sat *after* the clause, where an off-by-one only shifts the cut's far edge and the whitespace trim absorbs it. Moving an expansion into the text that must survive — "switch to Straße in the workspace Alpha" — makes the same map cut a character off the wrong side, and M22 dies. Recorded because the first battery had the mirror-image case (M5's no-op mutant, which needed the *mutant* fixed rather than the test), and the two together are the reason a survivor is never left unexamined.

**Mutation battery: 22 designed, 22 killed, plus one neutrality check that correctly survived.** Run against the committed tree per round (`461326e` for SONNY-68's eleven, `d1917a3` for SONNY-48's five, `b2a1856`/`eda5e74` for the cycle-2 round's six), each mutant reverted with `git checkout -- Sources/` and the tree status-verified clean before the next. SONNY-68: M1 resolver narrowing removed entirely → 6 killing tests; M2 clause subtraction only → 6; M3 the article and " app" trims only → 4; M4 `switch_running_app` re-excluded from the schema → the schema-shape test and the §A4 pin; M5 its `plannerTools` emptied → both goldens, `ToolRegistryTests` and the pin; M6 dropped from `forbiddenStepOperations` → the eight-operation list test; M7 the second clause word order removed → 5; M8 the new prompt rule deleted → the system-prompt golden; M9 the `routineSteps` sentence reverted → the same golden; M10 clause subtraction dropping the text after the clause instead of rejoining it → the clause-removal test; M11 the recognizer returning the raw typed name instead of the canonical saved one → 6, including four pre-existing tagging tests. SONNY-48: M12 `save_snippet` re-excluded → the schema test and the pin; M13 its `plannerTools` emptied → 4; M14 its prompt rule deleted → the golden; M15 `expand_snippet` given a planner tool, the boundary in the other direction → 5; M16 `.saveSnippet` added to `forbiddenStepOperations` → 6, including SONNY-31's own `aScheduledSnippetRoutineStillRunsOnItsSecondOccurrence`, which is the sharpest available evidence that SONNY-48's story and SONNY-31's are one story. **N1, the neutrality check:** removing the "does this command contain the word workspace at all" pre-check leaves the suite green, which is the evidence that it is an optimisation rather than a behaviour change — a mutant that survives on purpose, recorded as such so a later reader does not mistake it for a coverage hole. **Cycle-2 round:** M17 the shipped F1 defect reintroduced (the unconditional article trim ahead of the guard) → killed by the base-parity table and the naming-form test; M18 the naming form widened back into a bare article rule on the clause path → killed by the base-parity table, which is what proves the gate is load-bearing and not decoration; M19 the naming form removed outright → killed by 4, observation 2 among them; M20 edge punctuation no longer trimmed → killed by the punctuation test; M21 the prompt rule re-forbidding `open_workspace` → killed by the golden *and* by the both-directions test, which is the point of having both; M22 the index map replaced by a naive same-length assumption → **survived first, killed after the test was fixed** (see the pitfall above). **Two mutants were run twice, for opposite reasons, and both are recorded because a battery's value is entirely in whether its mutants actually mutate and its tests can actually fail**: M5's first form wrote `[] as [AgentTool] + [tool]`, the same array, so the *mutant* was a no-op and re-running it correctly killed it by four tests; M22's first run was a genuine survivor and the *test* was what needed strengthening.

Known limitations / deferred scope:
- **The planner half is planner judgment, and the tests pin only what can be pinned.** That `switch_running_app` exists in the schema, is described to the model, and carries a rule naming the misroute is asserted exactly; that the model *chooses* it for "bring me back to Slack" is not, and cannot be by a unit test. That is manual-test item 7 on SONNY-68 and, in the longer run, the kind of thing SONNY-72's planner benchmark exists to measure.
- **`focus on X in my Y workspace` still falls to the planner.** The leading-stop-word guard rejects "on …" by design — it is what keeps "focus on writing my essay" off the running-app matcher — so that phrasing is caught by the planner half rather than the resolver half. Deliberate: weakening the guard to claim it would trade a routing bug for a false-claim bug.
- **The prompt's `routineSteps` exclusion sentence still names five of the eight forbidden operations**, omitting `create_workspace`, `edit_workspace` and `open_workspace`. Adding `switch_running_app` to it was required by this branch; naming the other three would change what the planner attempts for "teach me a routine that opens my research workspace", a routine-authoring product decision this branch has no business making. Filed as **SONNY-74** (Backlog, untriaged).
- **Two normalisations reach the guard, and only one of them is a strict no-op against base.** Clause subtraction cannot change a clause-free command at all. Edge-punctuation trimming can, and does so deliberately (F3) — including in one degenerate way worth naming rather than discovering: a trailing punctuation *word* ("switch to x y z .") counts toward the three-word ceiling at `48d0150` and does not here, so a four-token remainder can become a three-token one. That is a word-count change, not a stop-word change, the base-parity table's subject is the stop words, and the direction is fail-closed either way — but "the no-clause path is byte-identical to base" would have been a blanket claim, and it is not one.
- **`AgentActionExecutor.previewNestedPlan` routes to `preview(plan:)`, which alone among the executor's entry points never calls `resolveDefaultOutputs`.** Moot today precisely because `switch_running_app` is banned from routines — nothing that needs pinning can reach it — but it is the same shape the ban exists to contain, one layer further in, and the next operation to leave the exclusion list has to look at it. Raised by PR #39's cycle-1 review as noted-not-filed; recorded here rather than turned into a ticket because there is no reachable defect to fix, only a trap to know about.
- **A scoped switch decrypts `WorkspaceStore` twice per submission** — once for the resolver's clause subtraction, once in `resolveTaskScope`. Accepted rather than cached: the two reads happen at different layers with different lifetimes, a shared cache would be new mutable state on a path whose whole virtue is that it has none, and the literal-noun pre-check already skips the read entirely for every command that cannot carry a clause. Named so the cost is a decision on the record and not an oversight.
- **The prompt's "For X, produce…" rules do not uniformly follow adapter registration order**, and this branch's own commit message and two ticket comments said they did. 23 of 24 follow; `create_local_draft` (`OpenAIPlanner.swift:158`, adapter 8) precedes `open_generated_artifact` (`:159`, adapter 7). Pre-existing, untouched, and the placement chosen for the two new rules is right either way — the defect was the unchecked universal, which is exactly CLAUDE.md's count-the-whole-population rule. Corrected on both tickets. (PR #39 review, cycle 1, F4.)
- **A workspace named the same as a verb still wins on the bare word.** With a workspace called "Switch" saved, the command "switch" is an exact saved-name match and quick dispatch opens the workspace before the running-app prefixes are consulted. Unchanged by this branch, now asserted in the fixture so it reads as precedence rather than a bug; the bare verb's clarification stays pinned in `RunningAppAndRecentArtifactsTests` against a store with no such collision.

Open questions (required, write "none" if true): none. SONNY-48's direction (A versus B) was the one open product question and the founder answered it — direction A, the planner learns `save_snippet` — as did the veto this session offered on `switch_running_app`'s routine containment, which was kept. Both exchanges are now recorded on their tickets as question-and-answer with dates, rather than only inside the prose of the session that acted on them: PR #39's cycle-1 review filed that single-witness shape as a convention finding, and it was right to (SONNY-48, F5).

At the cycle-2 fix head: **790 / 60, exit 0**. Net +39 tests, +2 suites. **Five test functions disappear against base and all five are replacements, not removals** — `git diff dfafac6..HEAD -- 'Tests/*' | grep '^-' | grep 'func '` returns exactly those five, each the compose-era name of a behaviour that no longer exists because the API it tested was deleted. **"Rename" is the wrong word for all four and is corrected here**: every one had a materially rewritten body, because the API under test was gone; three of the four gained assertions, and one lost one.
