Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**"Run again" re-asks and never replays, and the reason to record is the gate rather than the coordinates** (founder, 2026-08-16). Sonny's gate is pre-execution and whole-plan: `AgentRunner.execute` assesses once, up front, and `executeChain` runs every segment with no re-gating. So re-executing a previously approved plan would carry an approval granted for a world that has since changed — the file that did not exist then exists now, so the destructive escalation that should fire would not. Re-asking through the planner keeps every gate honest by construction rather than by anyone remembering. The two secondary reasons, recorded as secondary: nothing in this codebase replays a stored plan today (both existing repeat mechanisms re-derive from an identifier), and a screen-control replay would click at coordinates that have moved.

**Re-asking re-resolves the workspace binding and re-requests approval, by design** (founder, same date). A task that asked for permission the first time asks again. This will read as a regression to anyone expecting a one-click repeat, which is exactly why it is written down: it is the same property that makes replay unsafe, seen from the user's side. The consequence rule then governs the second run on its own merits — an action that was not destructive in March may be destructive today.

**Running again a screen-control task starts a fresh session and replays nothing.** The stored command is re-planned, may resolve to a vision session again, and is gated as any new vision command is — the terminal deny list, the consequence rule, Safe mode's floor, unattended-never. The journal is **a record of what happened, not a script**, and this is written down because "retry a screen-control task" reads like replaying the clicks and replaying stored clicks blind is precisely the unsafe thing. Pinned end to end: two sessions with different ids, the first byte-for-byte what it was, the new row pointing at the new one.

**The persistence security note — row I's lesson, widened along a new axis.** `PriorTaskContext.plannerContextText` escaped `previousCommand` and `planSummary` and skipped `outcome.plannerText` and `step.plannerText`. Harmless while every run summary was a code-authored adapter string; not harmless once row I shipped a capability whose summary is free text written by a model that had just read the user's screen — and the vision prompt actively asks the model to describe what it saw, so the designed response to an injection attempt was to transcribe it into the one field that reached the trusted block unescaped. **Persistence removes the ten-minute bound that made the original omission survivable.** Two structural answers, not two remembered ones: stored fields reach a planner **only** by being built into a `PriorTaskContext` through its own initialisers, so `escapeForPlanner` is inherited rather than applied; and the stored result carries a provenance-declaring type, because "a structural guarantee is only as wide as the type that carries it" is the row I sentence this row is the test of. **The honest limit, stated so nobody over-reads it:** the type declares provenance and **cannot verify redaction**, because by the time it exists the value is already a plain `String` — `VisionSessionOutcome.Ending.summary` de-redacts at `VisionSessionRunner.swift:34,37` before it ever becomes `AgentRunResult.summary`. Do not make `RedactedPayload` `Codable` to close that: a `Decodable` conformance is a public initialiser in disguise, and its own comment says so. The precedent copied instead is `RedactionReportEntry` — `Codable` by design while the payload it summarises is not.

**Provenance is declared where the text is authored, and two sites forward rather than author.** Enumerated at `ebd6c1d`: 27 `AgentRunResult(` construction sites in `Sources/`, 26 code-authored templates and exactly one — `VisionSessionCapabilityAdapter.swift:278` — carrying free text a model composed. `AgentActionExecutor.executeChain` joins one summary per chain segment and `RunRoutineCapabilityAdapter` wraps a nested run's summary in a sentence of its own; both carry the provenance forward, because declaring either `.codeAuthored` on the ground that *it* wrote the template would launder the model's text. Of the two only the chain is **reachable today** — a plan may mix ordinary steps with a vision step, which `visionSplitDisclosure` writes a sentence describing, while `StoredRoutine.forbiddenStepOperations` refuses `.visionSession` inside a routine outright. The unreachability was established rather than assumed: the first draft of the routine test seeded such a routine and failed with `unsafeRoutineStep("vision_session")`. The forwarding stays anyway, because a hardcoded `.codeAuthored` becomes wrong silently the day a second model-authored capability exists.

**The line the provenance enum draws is who composed the prose, not whether any substring came from a model** — and it has to be stated, because the looser reading makes the enum useless. Nearly every code-authored summary interpolates a value a planner chose ("Zipped 3 files to …/large-files.zip" gets its path from the plan), and so does an error's own description: `VisionDecisionParseError.unknownAction` prints the action name the model asked for inside a sentence this repository wrote. Under a "contains nothing model-derived" reading almost nothing would qualify. Under this one the cases separate the thing that matters: `.modelAuthored` text can be an entire injected paragraph, while a `.codeAuthored` template bounds a model's contribution to the slots it interpolates. Escaping is unconditional either way.

**The heavy half of the record went to a store of its own, and the decision reversed on a measurement** (founder, 2026-08-17, superseding his own of 2026-08-16). The earlier choice — result, plan summary and steps all on `CompletedTaskRecord` — was made on a privacy argument that remains correct: a side store buys little when the backend retains the same content for 30–90 days, and the local copy is the one the user can actually delete. What was missing was a measurement. SONNY-119 then took one at `36cef9e`: the unsplit shape reaches **38.81 MiB** at the 10,000-record cap with `record(_:)` at **307 ms**, against **3.53 MiB** and **130 ms** today — "roughly triples" measured as about **11×**, and these stores are whole-file encrypted, so that is ~39 MB decrypted on every read and re-encrypted on every finished task.

**What the split actually buys is the reads, not the writes, and saying otherwise would invite a later reader to undo it.** A finished task now writes two files instead of one and the summed bytes are similar. The gain is that `TaskHistoryStore.loadAll()` runs several times per task — inside `record(_:)` itself, again in `refreshTaskHistory()`, and again for the Tasks list, search and Insights — while the plan store is read only when someone opens one task's detail or arms a follow-up on it. Moving ~1.7 kB of plan text per record out of the file that is read constantly and into the one that is read almost never is where the time goes. That reasoning lives on `TaskPlanDetailStore`'s own doc comment.

**The split is for size and never for lifetime, and the alignment is built rather than asserted.** The founder's objection to splitting was that "follow-ups on older tasks quietly get weaker with no way to say so" — a silent degradation the product cannot explain under the no-explanatory-copy rule. That objection binds only if the new store outlives its rows by less, so it must not: same cap (read off `TaskHistoryStore.defaultMaxItems` rather than repeated), same oldest-first-by-`completedAt` rule, deleted with the row, suppressed with the row. Same *eviction* needed more than a matching rule, because the two stores stay level only while every row has a plan — and a run that failed before preparing one writes a row with none, so the plan store would fill more slowly, evict later, and keep the plans of tasks the user can no longer see. So `TaskHistoryStore.record(_:)` now returns the ids it evicted and the plan store drops those **in the same write it was making anyway**. Zero extra writes; a demonstrated property rather than a coincidence.

**Two caps, both new, both with their arithmetic.** The result is capped at **1,000 characters**: record size is additive in that field (SONNY-119's own table has "+ result 200 chars, 8 steps" at exactly 374 + 200 + its 1,729 B of steps), so 1,000 bounds a record at ~1.4 kB and the hot file at ~13 MiB at the cap, against the 3.78 MiB SONNY-119 measured today's records at. The plan detail is capped by **one 2,500-character budget** plus a 400-character per-field ceiling — one budget rather than a product of five per-field caps, because a product is a bound nobody can hold in their head: twenty steps at 400 characters of description with sixteen details of 400 each is 136 kB an entry and 1.36 GB at the store's cap — technically bounded, practically not. Steps are kept whole and the remainder dropped, so a truncated plan is a prefix of the real one rather than a mangled version of all of it. Both caps also run on the **decode** path, so a value that reached a file by some other route is bounded when it is read back.

**The one unbounded producer is what motivates the result's cap at all.** Twenty-six of the 27 summary producers are short templates; the vision session's is free text a model wrote. And `TaskHistoryStore.record(_:)` decodes and re-encrypts the entire file on every finished task, so one pathological response would not merely be large once — it would tax every future task for as long as it stayed in the window.

**Why results are stored locally at all, now that the backend retains model traffic.** The founder's decision of 2026-08-16 has the server keeping requests and responses for 30–90 days. That is **not the same thing** as what a task produced and is not a substitute for it, and this is written down so a later reader does not "simplify" task detail into a server read. Three reasons: server traffic is prompts and completions, not the product's own record of a run's outcome; the local copy works offline, and the product is local-first; and the two retention clocks differ, so a task the user can still see could have no server-side record left at all.

**Why no side store was the earlier answer, and why one exists anyway.** The codebase argues for a side store in writing — `TaskHistoryStore.swift:39-41` states the pattern unprompted ("The record holds the link, the side store holds the content"), and `docs/sonny-v1-vision-planner-integration-plan.md:520` posed this exact fork for rows D/E three weeks earlier. The 2026-08-16 decision declined it for three reasons: row J's SONNY-140 already claims the tenth store and already rewrites `theWipeReachesExactlyTheNineLocalStores`, so a row E store would be the eleventh with both rows editing one test; the privacy case is weaker than it looks now that the backend retains command text anyway; and a side store's own cost is follow-ups quietly degrading on older tasks with no way to say why. The 2026-08-17 measurement overturned the first and third: **the store exists, and it neutralises the third by sharing the row's retention exactly.** The first became bookkeeping — row E landed first, so the count is **ten** and row J's SONNY-140 now raises the number rather than setting it, in `theWipeReachesExactlyTheTenLocalStores` and `everyLocalStoreFileIsClassifiedExactlyOnce`.

**The armed follow-up's lifecycle, and the two obvious alternatives that are both wrong.** An armed context keeps the original task's real timestamp and is exempt from the ten-minute expiry, because it was armed by a deliberate user action rather than left behind by the last run. Stamping the original `createdAt` on an unexempted context **silently kills the feature**: `currentContext()` self-clears on read, so a task from yesterday is dropped on the very next read and the follow-up reaches the planner with no context at all, looking from the outside exactly like it worked. Stamping `Date()` instead puts a **false `Captured at:`** inside the trusted block — the one segment the planner's own system prompt describes as authoritative. **Exemption from the timer is not permission to persist:** `consumeArmedContext()` spends it at the moment `performStart` reads it, explicitly rather than leaving it to the `record(...)` that usually overwrites it later, because "usually overwritten later" is a different promise from "spent now" and the gap between them is a follow-up silently attaching itself to the command after this one. Nothing persists an arm across launches.

**The two fallback strings stopped asserting a cause.** `plannerContextText` emitted "- unavailable; prior task failed before preparation completed" and "- none available; prior task failed before preparation completed" for an empty plan summary and empty steps. That names a cause that is only sometimes the reason, and row E made the other case the common one: every task recorded before this row has no stored plan, so a follow-up on a **completed** one would have put those two lines directly above `Previous outcome: completed - …` — a flat contradiction inside the trusted block. They now read "- not recorded" and "- none recorded", true of the live no-plan case and the rehydrated pre-row-E case alike.

**Two chips became three, so the chips got a row of their own** (founder, 2026-08-21). Three chips inline in a 472-point pill leave the text field about **57 points** wide — an estimate from the chips' own text and padding, and the basis the decision was taken on — at the exact moment the user is typing a correction into it. The pill now grows from 40 to 66 whenever any chip is on and is unchanged when none is. The two declined alternatives are recorded because both are tempting: hard-truncating the follow-up chip keeps one row and still leaves the field around 90 points, and a chip that names no task fits easily but reintroduces the invisible state the chip exists to prevent — an invisible trusted block reaching the planner is worse than an invisible workspace binding, which is the case that slot already existed to prevent. Order is the two that were there first, then the new one: compose, do not displace. One consequence had to be handled rather than discovered — the two circular buttons beside the pill were centred against it and would have floated 13 points above the field; they now sit in a 40-point box of their own, bottom-aligned, which is exactly level in both heights and pixel-identical when no chip is on.

**The sheet's height stopped being a branch and became a sum.** With two optional sections the old `record.visionSessionID == nil ? 320 : 560` ternary is a four-case arithmetic, and row D is still adding controls to the same dialog. It is now `base + Σ(present sections)`, and the result section's own share is **derived from its text** rather than fixed, because a fixed allowance either clips a long result or leaves most of a hundred points of white under a short one. The line count is an estimate — nothing outside a live layout pass knows where text wraps — and the block is built so both ways of being wrong are mild: the view gives its scrolling content exactly the height the sheet reserved, so an under-estimate scrolls instead of clipping, and the sheet's existing `Spacer(minLength: 20)` absorbs an over-estimate. Content-sizing the sheet was the sanctioned alternative and was declined for a concrete reason: the screen-record section contains a `ScrollView` whose greediness is currently masked by the fixed height, and **no agent in this repository can look at the result**, so a layout change resting on reasoning alone was the wrong trade.

**A record with nothing to show renders nothing at all.** Row I's rule for the vision section, extended, and it holds harder here: every record written before row E has no stored result, so this is the common path on day one rather than an edge, and an empty state would tell each of those users their task produced nothing when the truth is that Sonny was not keeping results yet — a truth the no-explanatory-copy rule forbids writing down beside it. Two histories collapse into one `nil` in `TaskDetailPresentation.resultText`, so no branch in the body can drift apart.

**The stored plan steps are not rendered to anyone.** They are context for the planner. A list of internal step descriptions on a user-facing receipt is the surface the founder rejected on 2026-07-18 ("logs + summary + activity should just be a flow").

**A tenth store means eleven test fixtures, and the trap is the one this repo has already recorded twice.** Every `AgentViewModel` fixture in `Tests/` injects its own `taskHistoryStore` under a temporary root. A tenth store defaulting to `~/Library/Application Support/Sonny/task-plan-details.json` would have had eleven fixtures writing to the developer's real data — hermetic by accident rather than by construction, which is exactly what the journal's own fixture comments describe. All eleven now inject it.

**The wipe copy is unchanged, and that is a judgment rather than an oversight.** Settings' two enumerations of what a local-data wipe deletes name nine kinds and now cover ten files. The tenth is not a new kind: a task's plan is keyed on that task's row, capped with it, evicted with it, deleted with it and suppressed with it, so "task history" covers it in the user's terms. Row I's screen record earned its own clause because it is genuinely a different thing — a record of the user's screen rather than of Sonny's own bookkeeping. Recorded here so a reviewer can disagree with the judgment rather than find a silent gap; SONNY-109 can overrule it.

**One defect found and filed rather than absorbed — SONNY-195.** A run bound to a workspace whose name its command does not contain writes a task-history row tagged with **no workspace**. `resolveTaskScope` prefers `explicitWorkspaceBinding`; the row's tag comes from `WorkspaceTaskTagging.resolvedWorkspaceName(command:plan:…)`, which reads the plan's workspace steps and the command text and never the binding. Pre-existing, and it reaches every dispatch that binds explicitly — the workspace card's "New task in …" flow included, where the widget chip says "In Research" for the whole run and the row afterwards says nothing. Outside SONNY-149's scope, so it is a discovery ticket; `runningAgainCarriesTheRecordsWorkspaceWhenItStillExists` asserts the `nil` deliberately with a comment pointing at it, so nobody later reads the absence as something run-again broke.

Known limitations / deferred scope:
- **Results are not backfilled onto older records, and never will be.** That information is gone, and inventing it would be worse than its absence. Task detail therefore stays a bare receipt for everything that ran before this row — the common case for a while — and a follow-up on such a record has the command and the outcome but no plan. The product says so by rendering nothing, not by explaining.
- **No wireframe exists for this surface.** `docs/wireframes/` holds one file, `15-SegmentedControl.svg`, unrelated to task detail. Everything here — the Result block, the two footer actions, the chip row — is net-new System A (and System B for the chip) on session judgment, with the widget's chip layout and copy founder-approved on 2026-08-21 and everything else settled by **SONNY-109**'s whole-product pass.
- **A follow-up on a task whose plan store will not read** arms with the command and the outcome, reports the load failure in the usual banner, and is honest about having less to go on. Refusing to arm would trade a degraded feature for no feature, and the founder's objection to a shorter-lived detail store was precisely that follow-ups must not *quietly* get weaker.
- **Deleting a task removes the backend's copy too, and a task marked "Don't save this task" is never retained server-side** — both row 12's, on SONNY-16 and SONNY-134. Row E adds no client seam for either: a stored result and a stored plan are deleted and suppressed by riding a record row D already classifies as a trace.
- The result block's line estimate, and every question about how the two new surfaces actually look, are the founder's manual pass. No agent in this repository can screenshot or drive the live app.

Open questions (required, write "none" if true): none. SONNY-195 is filed and untriaged, which is a queued item rather than an open question.

Manual checklist for the founder (packaged app):
1. Run a task that produces a file, open its detail: the Result block says what it produced, wraps, and can be selected.
2. Open a task from before this shipped: no Result block at all — no heading, no empty sentence.
3. Open a task with both a result and a screen record: both sections there, nothing clipped, no large gap above the footer. Then a task with a long result: past about six lines the block scrolls rather than the sheet growing.
4. Open a failed task: the failure text is there.
5. Press **Run again**: it runs, and the Tasks page shows it in progress. Run again a task that needed approval — it asks again (intended). Run again one bound to a workspace you have since deleted — it runs unscoped and does not error. Start a task, then open a detail sheet: both footer actions are visibly disabled, and enabled again when it ends.
6. Run again a screen-control task: a new session starts and drives the app live; nothing about it looks like a recording being played back.
7. Press **Follow up** on an old task: the widget comes forward with an empty box and a chip naming the task. Type a correction and submit — it does the corrected thing. Leave one armed fifteen minutes, then submit — it still works. Arm, submit, then submit an unrelated command — the second is unaffected. Arm one and dismiss the chip — the next command is unaffected.
8. With a workspace binding and "Don't save this task" also on, confirm all three chips are readable together and the two circular buttons stay level with the text field. Then confirm the pill is unchanged — 40 tall, no chip row — whenever no chip is on.
9. Run a task, quit, relaunch, open its detail: the result is still there. The encrypted round trip on a real store rather than a fixture.

Next branch: row J (`SONNY-140`'s approved-apps store) now raises the local-store count to eleven rather than setting it to ten. SONNY-109's whole-product UI/UX pass owns the final wording and layout of everything this row put on screen.

**PR #89 CYCLE-1 FIX ROUND, appended 2026-08-21. The review found no shipped defect — the behaviour above is what shipped and the security trace holds — and four guards these tickets required pinned that a mutation battery showed were not. Everything above stands; this block records what the round changed and why the round was possible at all.**

**The shape of the finding, which is the durable half.** Four separate places where a ticket named a property, a test existed with a name that claimed it, and a mutant deleting the property survived the whole suite. Not one of them was a missing test. Each was a test that passed for a reason other than the one its name asserts — the failure mode this repository's evidence rules exist for, arriving in the branch that wrote those rules' latest instalment.

- **`consumeArmedContext` was held by nothing** (M4). SONNY-150 required both halves of the arm's lifecycle pinned; the expiry half was, the spent half was not. `anArmedContextIsSpentByOneRunAndTheNextCommandSeesNoTraceOfIt` passes with the method gutted, because the follow-up's own terminal `recordPriorTaskContext` overwrites the stored context a moment later — which is **precisely** the "usually overwritten later is not the same promise as spent now" gap the method was written to close, quoted in its own doc comment. A test that cannot distinguish the mechanism from the coincidence it was built to replace holds neither.
- **The eviction handoff's plan-less branch was untested in both copies** (M6, M6s). `theHistoryStoreReportsWhatItEvictedAndThePlanStoreDropsThoseInTheSameWrite` writes a plan on every row, so it exercises the branch that already worked. The branch that fires when a run failed before preparing a plan — the exact scenario "same cap, same eviction" exists for, since that run writes a row with none — could be deleted in both the foreground and the scheduled path with the suite still green.
- **The plan store's own eviction backstop was dead to the suite, and its test asserted the opposite of its name** (M8). Three entries against a ten-thousand cap, a local variable named `overCap` holding three, and a closing assertion that nothing had been evicted. It read like coverage from every angle except the one that counts.
- **`AgentEvent.swift` named a test that has never existed** (M9b). `theOnlyModelAuthoredRunSummaryIsTheVisionSessions` was cited as the guard on `summaryProvenance`'s `.codeAuthored` default; `grep` returns one hit, the citation. Worth recording precisely because the first mutant written for it *died*: adding `.modelAuthored` to the calculator adapter is caught, since two fixtures run the calculator and read its provenance back. Moving the same mutant to `RevealInFinderCapabilityAdapter` survived. **Coverage that happens to intersect a property is not a guard on it**, and a battery that stops at the first kill will not tell the two apart.

**What was added.** Three direct store-level tests for `consumeArmedContext`, calling it and asserting on the store rather than through a run that would overwrite it anyway. A foreground and a scheduled eviction test at a cap of two where the evicting row has **no** plan, each asserting both that the displaced row's plan is gone and that the evicting row really stored none — so neither can quietly drift onto the branch that already worked. `TaskPlanDetailStore.maxDetails` became an injectable instance property (the seam `TaskHistoryStore.maxItems` already has, for the reason its doc comment records), and the eviction test now exceeds a real cap, with a sibling pinning that eviction is by `completedAt` and not by write order — a distinction a chronologically-inserted fixture cannot see, and a mutant of its own. `RunSummaryProvenanceTests` enumerates every file in both targets for `.modelAuthored` declarations, in `MacAgentSource`'s comment-stripped scan shape; that scanner gained a core-source accessor rather than a second scanner being built in the other target, because two independently maintained copies of comment-stripping is the failure that file's own doc comment records twice.

**Two guards the seam itself now needs.** An injectable cap is a test seam, and shipping a shorter life through it is the one thing the founder's 2026-08-17 split condition forbids — follow-ups must not quietly get weaker on older tasks. So `noProductionPathPassesACapToThePlanStore` — named `theShippedPlanCapIsTheHistoryCapAndNoProductionPathOverridesIt` until cycle 3 renamed it, since the first half of that claim moved elsewhere and a name that overstates is a claim rather than a label — enumerates the three production construction sites and asserts none passes a cap, and `aPlanStoreBuiltWithZeroFloorsAtOneRatherThanErasingItself` pins the floor. The backstop's own doc comment now states why it is reachable rather than decorative: the handoff carries the evicted ids in the *same* write as the new detail, so a write that throws after the row write already landed loses them for good, and nothing re-derives them.

**One real inconsistency fixed alongside them.** The scheduled path wrapped both its writes in one `do`, so a failure of the *plan* write reported "Sonny could not save this scheduled run to task history" — false, the row was on disk — and skipped `refreshTaskHistory()`, leaving the row that did land absent from the published list until something else refreshed it. Two failures with different consequences and different recoveries now have two catches, two messages and a refresh that happens either way, matching what `recordTaskHistoryIfTerminal` and `recordTaskPlanDetail` already do for a foreground run. They are separate functions rather than one shared helper, so agreeing is something to do rather than something inherited. Pinned by a test that makes the plan store's directory read-only while task history stays writable — the fifth gated directory-locking test in the repository, which moved `TwinnedTestSupportTests`' population pin from four to five.

**And a records repair this branch caused.** SONNY-150 inserted `FollowUpPresentation` into `AgentActivityPresentation.swift` with no blank line after `TaskRecordingPresentation`'s doc block, so that block — the founder's not-Incognito reasoning, and the sentence claiming `TaskRecordingPresentationTests` refuses copy that reads like an explanation — documented the wrong enum, and `TaskRecordingPresentation` had none. Moved back. The same ticket's "compose with it, do not displace it" rule was written about the composer's chips and applies to the file just as well. The store-count sweep also found sites this branch had left at nine: `README.md` in five places, including the now-false "`LocalStorageEncryption` is the encryption/migration mechanism all nine share, not a tenth store" and a line SONNY-181 had itself corrected the day before; `LocalStoreClassification.swift` twice; and `VisionSessionJournalStore.swift`, which still named `theWipeReachesExactlyTheNineLocalStores` after this branch renamed it. Rows D and I's changelog entries correctly say nine and are left: a changelog is history. **This sentence said "two of nine sites" and recorded the sweep as complete, and it was not** (PR #89 cycle 2, F3) — two more sites stayed at nine while everything around them went to ten: `AgentViewModel.visionSessionJournalStoreForThisRun`'s doc comment, which carried *three* stale numbers at once ("the fifth `.trace` store", now the sixth; "the most sensitive of the nine"; and a quotation of the very `LocalStoreClassification` sentence this round had changed to "of the ten"), and `LocalStorageSecurityTests`' own count-assertion comment, which said "nine is now stated in a third place" eight lines above `#expect(fileURLs.count == 10)`. Both fixed. **The lesson is the one this branch keeps relearning about its own sweeps**: a count restated in prose is a copy, every copy is a place to go stale, and a sweep is complete when the pattern returns only history — not when the session stops finding hits. The comment in the security test now deliberately does not spell the number a second time, because a sentence that names it is one more copy to update.

**Two discovery tickets, both about the trusted block and neither fixed here.** **SONNY-197** — `followUpOnTask` drops `record.result?.provenance`, because `PriorTaskOutcome` has no provenance field, so a stored model-authored paragraph enters the planner's trusted block indistinguishable from a template. Not a defect: escaping is unconditional and nothing reads the flag yet, and `PriorTaskContext`'s live path was never-touch for SONNY-150. It is the structural version of this row's own security note, one axis further. **SONNY-198** — `escapeForPlanner` neutralises the two delimiter tokens and nothing else, and the trusted block is line-oriented, so a stored result containing a newline can forge a `Previous command:` line *inside* an intact wrapper. Every trim on the path is `.whitespacesAndNewlines`, which does not touch an interior newline. Pre-existing since row I and out of scope here — but row E is what removed the ten-minute bound on it, and the one model-authored producer writes multi-line prose as its ordinary case, so it is recorded against this row rather than left where nobody would look.

**Batteries, both directions, at their SHAs.** Before, at `dccf45c`: five mutants, four survived — M4, M6, M6s, M8 — with M9's calculator variant killed and its honest form M9b confirmed surviving in a second run. After, at `7d164df`: **nine mutants, nine killed, none survived**, each by the test written for it — M4 by `consumingAnArmedContextSpendsItImmediately`, M6 by `aRowWithNoPlanStillDropsThePlanOfTheRowItEvicted`, M6s by `aFailedScheduledRunWithNoPlanStillDropsThePlanOfTheRowItEvicted`, M8 by both new eviction tests, M8b by the by-`completedAt` one, M9b by `theOnlyModelAuthoredRunSummaryIsTheVisionSessions`, M10 and M11 by `aPlanWriteFailureKeepsTheScheduledRowAndSaysWhatActuallyFailed`, M12 by `consumingIsANoOpOnAnOrdinaryContext`. M8b, M10, M11 and M12 were added for this round as the near-misses the new tests should also hold, rather than only re-running the four that failed.

Suite at `7d164df`: **1537 tests in 118 suites, exit 0** via the flagged command, against 1523 in 117 at `dccf45c`, and 1537/118 again at `1124b0e` and at this stamping commit — re-run rather than carried, though both are confined to this file. `scripts/warnings`: **0 at `7d164df`** and **0 at `1124b0e`**, every file compiled both times; not re-run for the stamping commit, whose diff is this paragraph.

**What the reviewer confirmed sound and this round deliberately did not touch:** the full security trace (all four interpolated fields escape; M1/M2/M7 killed), `StoredTaskResult`'s no-bypass structure, the split-for-size reasoning on every axis, SONNY-149's no-in-flight-guard argument, SONNY-148's renders-nothing rule, the five figures the previous round corrected, fixture hermeticity, and the wipe-copy judgment.

**PR #89 CYCLE-2 FIX ROUND, appended 2026-08-21.** Two survivors and a records repair. Both survivors are cycle 1's *own* fixes failing to hold, which is the finding worth keeping: a round that adds guards adds claims, and those are as fresh and as unchecked as the ones they replaced.

**M13 — the founder's split condition was not actually guarded.** Shipping `maxDetails: Int = TaskHistoryStore.defaultMaxItems / 2` — a 5,000 plan cap against a 10,000 history, which is exactly the shorter life the 2026-08-17 condition forbids — passed the whole suite. Two assertions that between them *looked* like a guard and were not, each defeated by a different mechanism:

- `theShippedPlanCapIsTheHistoryCapAndNoProductionPathOverridesIt` asserted the declaration `contains("...defaultMaxItems")`, and `defaultMaxItems / 2` contains it. **A source check on a declaration is satisfied by any expression containing the searched text.**
- `thePlanStoreCapsAtExactlyTheHistoryStoresNumber` read the value back — through `makePlanStore`, the fixture helper, which passes `maxDetails` *explicitly*. So it asserted a number the test itself had supplied and never once exercised the store's own default. **A value test that constructs its subject with the parameter under test is a tautology.**

Fixed the way the sibling one file over already had it: `TaskHistoryRetentionTests.theShippedCapIsTenThousandAndNoProductionPathOverridesIt` builds `TaskHistoryStore()` with no cap argument and reads `maxItems` back. The plan store's test now does the same in every production construction shape, and additionally asserts the two stores' numbers equal *each other* rather than each equalling a literal — so a change to one that misses the other fails, which is the property the split condition actually rests on. The source check stays, narrowed to the half it can hold (no *caller* supplies a cap) with a comment saying it is not the guard on the value.

**M14 — the enumeration counted one of the two ways Swift lets you write the thing.** `theOnlyModelAuthoredRunSummaryIsTheVisionSessions` searched for `summaryProvenance: .modelAuthored`, the labelled-argument form, so a second declaring site written as an assignment — `result.summaryProvenance = .modelAuthored` — passed it. Not hypothetical: that spelling already exists in this codebase, at `AgentActionExecutor.executeChain`'s join. The scan now counts both, which has a consequence worth stating rather than hiding: the chain join is now *in* the population, so the expected map names it, and the by-name forwarding test remains the thing that says which of the two sites authors and which forwards. A third test pins that both search terms are exercised and both still occur — a term matching nothing anywhere is a term nobody would notice had stopped working.

**F4 — the two write paths did not actually agree, and the mode was documented with no test.** Cycle 1 split the *scheduled* path's two write failures. The foreground one still called `setError`, and `publishLocalStorageLoadError`'s own doc comment records what that costs in so many words: routing a storage notice into `errorMessage` makes a **successful** task render as a failure, because `FloatingWidgetView` picks `.failure` ahead of `.result` and `finalSummary` is set before the record path runs. So a task that ran, produced its result and wrote its row showed "Could not save this task's plan: …" where its result belonged. It now uses `recordLocalStorageWriteFailure`, exactly as its scheduled twin does — a plan-persistence failure is a **degraded follow-up**, not a failed task: the run happened, the row landed, and what is lost is that a later follow-up will have this task's command and outcome but not its plan. The test written for it was red against the old channel and green after, and it is the sixth gated directory-locking test in the repository, which moved `TwinnedTestSupportTests`' population pin from five to six.

**F3 — the sweep that was recorded as complete was not.** Two sites stayed at nine while everything around them went to ten: `AgentViewModel.visionSessionJournalStoreForThisRun`'s doc comment, which carried **three** stale numbers at once ("the fifth `.trace` store", now the sixth; "the most sensitive of the nine"; and a quotation of the very `LocalStoreClassification` sentence cycle 1 had just changed to "of the ten"), and `LocalStorageSecurityTests`' count-assertion comment, which said "nine is now stated in a third place" eight lines above `#expect(fileURLs.count == 10)`. The cycle-1 addendum's sentence claiming the sweep found "two of nine sites" is corrected in place. **The durable lesson, which this branch has now relearned three times about its own sweeps: a count restated in prose is a copy, every copy is a place to go stale, and a sweep is complete when the pattern returns only history — not when the session stops finding hits.** The security test's comment now deliberately declines to spell the number a second time, on the ground that a sentence naming it is one more copy to update.

**One discovery ticket, and it is about the instrument rather than the code. SONNY-199** — two `WidgetMicHoverHintTests` flake under battery load (2 failures in 12 full-suite runs, both `visibleHint → nil`), and **a flake and a kill are the same observation to a mutation battery**. A mutant aimed at anything those tests touch reads as killed when the suite was red for an unrelated timing reason — the reassuring direction, and the dangerous one. Until it is fixed the workaround is to **read the killer names, not the count**, which is how both of this PR's batteries were checked: every kill in the nine-mutant round at `7d164df` and the six-mutant round at `3fe718d` names a test written for that mutant, and neither flaky test appears as a killer anywhere. Nothing in row E goes near that surface; it surfaced here only because this branch ran more full-suite executions back to back than an ordinary branch does.

**Battery, both directions, at their SHAs.** Before, at `8689256`: two mutants, **both survived**. After, at `3fe718d`: **six mutants, six killed, none survived** — M13 by `thePlanStoreCapsAtExactlyTheHistoryStoresNumber`; M13b, a literal that *disagrees* with the constant (`= 9_000`), by the same test; M14 and M14b (the same second site in the other spelling) by `theOnlyModelAuthoredRunSummaryIsTheVisionSessions`; M16 (the channel reverted) by `aPlanWriteFailureLeavesTheTaskLookingSuccessfulAndSaysWhatActuallyFailed`; M17 (the foreground plan never written at all) by six tests. Four of the six were added for this round as near-misses the new tests should also hold.

**Corrected in cycle 3, because the sentence above did not reproduce as first written.** It described M13b as "a literal that happens to be right today, which the equality assertion catches and a `contains` never would" — and that parenthetical is *impossible*: a value-equality test cannot catch a literal equal to the constant it compares against. The mutant that actually ran under that id was `maxDetails: Int = 9_000`, a literal that disagrees, which the equality test kills for the obvious reason. The mutant the label describes is `maxDetails: Int = 10_000`, and it was never run. Run in cycle 3, at `f1b3c24`: it **SURVIVES**, and it is an **equivalent mutant** — behaviourally identical to the code it replaces, today, so no test can kill it and none should be written to try.

**Which does not leave the split condition unguarded, and the reason is worth having.** A hardcoded `10_000` is caught at the moment it starts to matter rather than at the moment it is written: the day the founder moves `TaskHistoryStore.defaultMaxItems`, the cross-store assertion `TaskPlanDetailStore().maxDetails == TaskHistoryStore().maxItems` fails, because one number moved and the other did not. That assertion is in the test precisely so the guarded property is the *relationship* between the two caps rather than each of them separately equalling a literal — which is why it was added in cycle 2 alongside the literal checks rather than instead of them. An equivalent mutant surviving is the expected outcome for a drift guard, and recording it as a kill was the error.

**And the class of the error is one this branch files tickets about.** A stamped battery figure that does not reproduce reads exactly like one that does; "six killed" was true of the mutants that ran and false of the mutants the entry described, which is the same shape as a test whose name claims more than its body — cycle 1's four findings, cycle 2's two, and now this. The label was written from the intent of the mutant rather than from its text, and nobody re-read the plan against the prose. **A mutant's note is a claim about the diff it applies, and it gets checked against that diff like any other measurement.**

Suite at `3fe718d`: **1539 tests in 118 suites, exit 0** via the flagged command, against 1537 in 118 at `8689256`, and 1539/118 again at `a438c51` and at this stamping commit — re-run rather than carried, though both are confined to this file. `scripts/warnings`: **0 at `3fe718d`** and **0 at `a438c51`**, every file compiled both times; not re-run for the stamping commit, whose diff is this paragraph.

**What cycle 2 confirmed sound and this round did not touch:** all nine of cycle 1's guard mutants still dead (M9b by the scan alone, with no fixture involved — item 4's property holds on its own), the shorter-cap-via-production-site enumeration, the floor test, the 4→5 tripwire, SONNY-197 and SONNY-198's accuracy, and the displaced doc block's repair.

**PR #89 CYCLE-3 TOUCH-UP, appended 2026-08-21.** Merge-ready on code; records, one dead assertion and two tickets. What it changed:

- **The M13b figure above, corrected in place** — the detail is in the cycle-2 block, and the short version is that a stamped battery figure did not reproduce because a mutant's *note* described a different diff than the mutant's *text*. Cycle 3 ran the mutant the note describes and it survives, as an equivalent mutant must.
- **A test line that could not fail**, in the test cycle 2 wrote for F4: `!hasVisibleWidgetPanel || errorMessage == nil`, whose right disjunct the line above already asserts, and whose left is false here regardless because the run's origin is `.commandCenter`. Replaced rather than deleted, with the premise the fix actually rests on: `FloatingWidgetView` picks `.failure` ahead of `.result`, so "the result stays on screen" holds only while that ordering does, and nothing in the suite pinned it. A mutant swapping the two arms is killed by the replacement, so it is not a second vacuous line.
- **A test renamed** — `theShippedPlanCapIsTheHistoryCapAndNoProductionPathOverridesIt` became `noProductionPathPassesACapToThePlanStore`, because cycle 2 moved the first half of that claim into `thePlanStoreCapsAtExactlyTheHistoryStoresNumber` and left the name promising a check the body no longer performs. Its doc comment already said so, which was not enough: a name is what a reader greps and what a failure prints.
- **One distance figure** in a doc comment, "twelve hundred lines up" for something about seven hundred lines up.

**Two tickets filed, both about guards rather than behaviour.** **SONNY-200** — the model-authored scan misses a *third* spelling (`var summaryProvenance: StoredTaskResult.Provenance = .modelAuthored`, the shape `executeChain` already uses for its accumulator), so a mutant flipping that declaration survives, and the enumeration's failure message overclaims by saying "in either spelling". The direction is safe — that mutant over-marks rather than under-marks, and nothing reads the flag to grant trust — but the ticket carries the deeper half: **no test runs an ordinary chain and asserts the join comes back `.codeAuthored`**, so the forward is pinned textually rather than behaviourally, and one behavioural test of that shape would kill the mutant regardless of spelling. **SONNY-201** — the foreground task-history *row*-write failure still calls `setError` while its scheduled twin uses the notice channel: the same class as F4, one line above F4's own fix, pre-existing and therefore out of this round's scope. Filed with the decision it needs rather than a patch, because a lost row is a heavier loss than a lost plan and someone may reasonably want it louder than a storage notice — in which case both paths move, not one.
